items.title: Bangladesh garment workers win 36pc wage rise
items.description: Bangladesh’s garment workers won a 36 per cent minimum wage increase on Wednesday, officials said, after weeks of sometimes violent protests causing hundreds of millions of dollars in business losses. The South Asian nation, the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, has seen widespread demonstrations since October by workers demanding higher pay. The garment industry, which clothes millions of consumers across Europe and North America, is Bangladesh’s economic lifeline, generating four-fifths of export earnings and employing more than four million people. After the deal was struck following lengthy negotiations with factory owners, workers’ representatives urged people to return to factories. “Although we are not completely satisfied, the outcome is not entirely bad either,” Babul Akhter, the labour representative on a wage board set up to resolve the crisis, told reporters. “Previously, workers used to get a wage revision every five years, but this time they are getting a revised wage after three years.” It was not immediately clear how workers — who clashed with police in industrial zones on Tuesday — would react to the deal. Workers initially demanded a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($240), up from 12,500 taka. They say their pay has failed to keep pace with the rising cost of food, housing, transport and health care. Judge Syed Azad Subhani, the chairman of the government-appointed garment industry wage board, said the “majority supported a minimum wage of 17,000 taka”, after a vote early Wednesday. The wage hike will take effect in January. ‘Export engine’ Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said on Sunday that protests had cost the industry an estimated $428 million, while orders worth $254m had shifted to other countries. The disruption came ahead of the busy Christmas season. The garment industry, which supplies major international brands including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss, earns around $38 billion a year. Bangladesh supplies more than 150 countries with ready-made garments, according to the BGMEA, which represents around 4,000 factories. The United States is its biggest individual market, while the European Union is its largest trading bloc. When Bangladesh won independence from Pakistan in 1971, it was among the world’s poorest countries, with its economy devastated by war. The expansion of garment production helped transform the nation of around 170 million people from a predominantly agricultural economy into a major global manufacturing hub. Bangladesh’s central bank calls the garment sector the “country’s export engine”. But its success has been built on a vast relatively low-paid workforce, with longstanding disputes over wages, working conditions and labour rights. The 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse, which killed more than 1,100 people and injured thousands, exposed appalling safety conditions in the industry, with workers employed in dangerous buildings and often lacking adequate labour protections. The disaster prompted major international efforts to improve workplace standards, including an agreement between global clothing brands and trade unions to inspect factories and enforce safety measures.

items.title: World: Health inequality monitoring atlas - A global mapping of country capacities, resources, policies and practices
items.description: Country: World Source: World Health Organization Please refer to the attached file. Countries face critical gaps in health inequality monitoring systems Health inequalities exist in every country. Yet millions of people at risk of being left behind may remain invisible in national health statistics. A new World Health Organization (WHO) report reveals that despite strong commitments, countries still face significant gaps in their ability to identify, measure and monitor health inequalities. The Health inequality monitoring atlas: a global mapping of country capacities, resources, policies and practices provides the first comprehensive global picture of national health inequality monitoring systems. Drawing on self-reported data from 161 WHO Member States, it highlights examples of encouraging progress and good practices, while also pointing to areas where further investment and support are needed. “Health inequality monitoring is an essential function that should be embedded in the health information systems of all countries,” said Dr Ahmad Reza Hosseinpoor, Health Inequality Monitoring Team Lead at WHO. “The release of this global atlas provides an important baseline snapshot of the situation in countries, and where countries can deepen efforts to strengthen the collection, analysis and use of inequality data for the advancement of health equity.” The findings expose a disconnect between ambition and action. While 89% of participating countries reported commitments to addressing health inequalities in national health sector strategic plans, only 65% had a ministry of health unit mandated to use inequality data and evidence. Even more striking, just one in five countries had published a dedicated national health inequality report in the previous decade. Although many countries routinely collect and report health data by age, sex and geographical location, information on economic status, education, ethnicity, disability and migration status remains far less available. This finding was evident across data sources such as health surveys, birth and death registrations, medical records and surveillance bulletins or dashboards. The Atlas also reveals disparities between countries. High-income countries generally have better systems for collecting, analyzing and reporting inequality data than low- and middle-income countries, but every country still has room for improvement and systems strengthening. Health inequality monitoring systems require continuous development as data systems, analytical methods and health challenges evolve. Every country has opportunities to strengthen how it generates, analyses and uses evidence on health inequalities. The Atlas identifies key priorities for strengthening health inequality monitoring systems, though these will differ according to the current maturity of health information systems and available resources. They include: leadership and strategic planning for the collection and use of health inequality data; inclusion of inequality measures within health goals and monitoring frameworks; protection and strengthening of health data infrastructure including the expanded collection of health inequality data; development of more integrated data systems, including expanding the use of electronic health records and establishing means for linking data across sources, while safeguarding data privacy and confidentiality; and strengthening of analytical and reporting capacity to track progress, evaluate the impact of policies and programmes, and inform action. WHO is supporting countries through technical assistance, capacity strengthening and practical resources available through the WHO Health Inequality Monitor . Support is also being expanded through the Health Inequality Monitoring Network and regional monitoring hubs. The Atlas establishes a crucial global baseline and a clear call to action: to close health inequalities, countries must first be able to see and measure them, then act on the evidence, so no one is deprived of the right to health.

items.title: Engrais : Fertial investit 35 millions de dollars pour propulser l’ammoniac algérien
items.description: L'Algérie ambitionne d'être un acteur incontournable dans le secteur stratégique des engrais et fertilisants. Pour ce faire, l'État à travers le groupe public Asmidal et sa filiale Fertial, ne lésine pas sur les moyens, afin de faire du pays, un pivot régional dans l'industrie des engrais. Algérie : 35 millions de dollars investis dans l’industrie des engrais avec l’expertise nationale En effet, Fertial a lancé un vaste programme de réhabilitation et de modernisation de ses unités d’ammoniac et d’engrais azotés. Doté d’une enveloppe de 35 millions de dollars, le projet est financé essentiellement sur les ressources propres de l’entreprise, avec un apport partiel d’Asmidal, sans recours aux crédits bancaires. Son PDG Riyad Sayad a déclaré au quotidien Annasr, cette démarche intervient après une période difficile marquée par le recul des capacités de production et l’insuffisance des investissements dans le renouvellement des installations. L’entreprise entend désormais privilégier la valorisation de ses ressources, la maîtrise des coûts et le recours aux compétences algériennes. À cet effet, les opérations de réhabilitation mobilisent 25 entreprises nationales, dont des start-ups, ainsi que 440 travailleurs et techniciens algériens. Le programme prévoit notamment 79 interventions techniques majeures sur les équipements industriels. Des capacités de production appelées à progresser Au-delà de la remise à niveau des installations, cette opération vise à améliorer sensiblement les performances industrielles du complexe. La production quotidienne d’ammoniac, qui se situait entre 550 et 600 tonnes avant 2024, a déjà progressé pour atteindre environ 750 tonnes. L’objectif est désormais de dépasser les 900 tonnes, avec une ambition de 1 000 tonnes par jour. Parallèlement, Fertial prévoit de porter le taux de disponibilité de ses installations de 64 % à 87 %, tout en assurant la conformité réglementaire de l’ensemble des équipements concernés. La maîtrise de la consommation énergétique constitue également un enjeu majeur. Le programme ambitionne de réduire la consommation spécifique de gaz naturel à moins de 1 300 m³ par tonne d’ammoniac produite, contre un niveau actuel nettement supérieur. Cette optimisation devrait également améliorer la rentabilité du complexe. Les projections économiques tablent ainsi sur plus de 16,77 milliards de dinars de gains cumulés sur cinq ans. La sécurité industrielle au cœur des opérations En parallèle de la modernisation des unités de production, Fertial a engagé le renouvellement de plusieurs infrastructures de transport d’ammoniac à Annaba. Les travaux portent notamment sur le remplacement de 3,6 kilomètres de conduites d’ammoniac gazeux, ainsi que sur la réhabilitation des installations de transport d’ammoniac liquide. Ces interventions s’inscrivent également dans une démarche de coordination avec le projet du terminal phosphatier du port d’Annaba qui a été lancé dans le cadre du projet intégré du phosphate de Bled el Hadba (Tébessa), afin d’assurer la compatibilité technique des deux infrastructures et de prévenir les risques industriels et environnementaux. Le programme de rénovation, entamé le 9 septembre 2026, doit se poursuivre jusqu’au 28 février 2027. De nouveaux engrais pour répondre aux besoins agricoles Enfin, Fertial entend diversifier son offre à travers le développement de nouvelles formulations d’engrais adaptées aux besoins du marché national. Parmi les pistes retenues figure le nitrate d’ammonium azotée, appelé à constituer une alternative à l’urée, dont la production est particulièrement consommatrice de gaz naturel. À travers ces différents chantiers, le complexe ambitionne de consolider sa place sur le marché national des engrais, tout en contribuant à l'approvisionnement du secteur agricole et aux objectifs de sécurité alimentaire du pays. items.title: Cuba: WHO Director-General's remarks at press conference – 24 November 2026
items.description: Country: Cuba Source: World Health Organization ¡Buenos días a todos! Muchas gracias for joining us. First, I want to thank the Government and people of Cuba for their warm welcome. I'm especially grateful to the Minister of Public Health, Dr José Ángel Portal Miranda, and his team. I'm also grateful to my WHO colleagues, our Assistant Director-General for Business Operations, Mr Raul Thomas; Our Regional Emergency Director for the Americas, Dr Ciro Ugarte; And my colleagues at the WHO-PAHO office here in Havana, led by Dr Mario Cruz. I also appreciated the opportunity to engage with the UN Resident Coordinator, the Country Team and members of the diplomatic community here in Havana. Cuba’s health system has a long and proud history. It's built on primary health care. It's universal. It trains health workers for dozens of countries. And it has a strong record of research and biotechnology. It’s a system built over generations, and must be protected. Yesterday I visited the William Soler Pediatric Hospital and its Cardiocenter. I met a little girl, just one year old, waiting for open-heart surgery. Her mother was by her side. I also met children waiting for operations, and doctors who know exactly what those children need. What they don't always have is the medicines, supplies, spare parts and reliable electricity they need to do it. Fuel and energy shortages, along with sanctions on buying medicines and equipment, have put serious pressure on these services. As the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, has warned, the tightening of fuel restrictions and sanctions is directly harming Cubans, especially the most vulnerable, and endangering lives, like the children I have already told you about earlier. He has called for these restrictions to be lifted immediately, and I echo that call. Cuba now has a backlog of almost 100 000 surgeries, including 12 000 children. We met some of those children. They should not have to wait for the care they need. 34 000 pregnant women cannot receive the care they need. And some important health indicators are moving in the wrong direction. Overall mortality has increased, and life expectancy in Cuba has decreased for the first time since records began in 1950, from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025. Infant mortality has more than doubled, from about 4 deaths per 1000 live births to 9.9 in 2025. Maternal mortality has also increased from 37.4 per 1000 live births in 2019 to 44.1 in 2025. Tuberculosis cases have also increased by 50% since 2019, along with outbreaks of Oropouche, dengue and chikungunya. The impact on children makes me especially sad. Childhood cancer survival rates have dropped from 85% to 65% following the onset of the energy blockade in January. During my visit to the Cardiocenter, I also met its founder, Dr Herminia Palenzuela. She's 80 years old, and she's still teaching the next generation of paediatric cardiologists. People like her are the reason this system keeps working. Hospitals have stayed open, and essential services keep running. Health workers come to work every day, often after long nights without power. They deserve more than our appreciation. They deserve our support. We were also briefed on the many challenges facing Cuba, including its health system, and on the 176 internal reform initiatives, understanding that it’s within Cuba’s interests to address its internal challenges. The reforms cover all sectors, including the economy, so WHO and the whole of the UN is committed to supporting these reforms as they relate to health and the other sectors. WHO is acting. At the hospital, we delivered medicines and medical supplies mobilized through PAHO's emergency programme. WHO has also provided 2 million US dollars in flexible funding. We agreed with the Minister to prioritize childhood vaccination, so that no child misses the protection they're entitled to. We'll also work with the Ministry to identify which medical equipment needs repair, and to mobilize additional resources for it. And we'll support Cuba's scientists. We'll work with the national regulatory authority and with Cuban vaccine and biotechnology institutions to speed up the WHO processes that can bring their products to more people. But no single agency can meet these needs alone. I call on our partners to increase their technical and financial cooperation with Cuba. The focus should be on what matters most right now: keeping services running, protecting children and mothers, and maintaining vaccination. Health should never be a casualty of politics. Children waiting for heart surgery should not have to wait for electricity. WHO will continue to stand with the people of Cuba and with the health workers who serve them. Once again, my thanks to the Minister, to all health workers, and to the Government and people of Cuba for their hospitality. Muchas gracias, and I look forward to your questions.

items.title: Pakistan calls for human control over decisions on nuclear weapons use
items.description: UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan has called for keeping decisions on the use of nuclear weapons under human control and warned that artificial intelligence (AI) systems must never be used to target nuclear command, control and communications systems. The warning was delivered by Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, during a high-level open debate of the UN Security Council on Wednesday on conflict resolution in an era of rapid technological change. The ambassador’s remarks carry particular significance for South Asia, where both Pakistan and India possess nuclear weapons, making the security of nuclear command, control and communications systems an important regional concern. “This is most critical in the nuclear domain, where decisions on the use of nuclear weapons must remain under human control, and AI systems must never be used to target nuclear command, control and communications systems,” Ambassador Shah said. He cautioned that the rapid development and convergence of emerging technologies were adding unprecedented speed, scale and complexity to international security challenges and could intensify the ongoing arms race. Ambassador Shah said technology itself was neutral, with its impact depending on the intentions and motivations of those using it. The foremost priority, he stressed, should be to retain human judgement and control at all stages of technological design, development and integration. He called for appropriate safeguards, regulations and governance frameworks to ensure that technological advances served peace rather than becoming instruments of geopolitical dominance and war. In the military domain, he advocated restraint and confidence-building measures to reduce the risks of miscalculation and compressed decision-making, particularly in the nuclear domain. The Pakistani envoy also warned against allowing advanced technologies to become the monopoly of a few powerful countries, arguing that all member states, including developing countries, should participate in their democratic, inclusive and equitable development. He said measures introduced in the name of technological safety should not become instruments for denying other countries access to technology and infrastructure. All member states, particularly developing countries, retained their inalienable right to the peaceful use of technology, he added. Shah also highlighted the growing dangers of misinformation, disinformation, fake news and cyberattacks, including attacks on critical infrastructure by state and non-state actors. “The UN Charter and international law apply in all situations, irrespective of underlying technologies,” he said, calling for collective efforts to clarify the application of international law and take concrete action against emerging threats. He advocated practical confidence-building measures, including crisis communication, deconfliction and mutual restraint, to reduce mistrust, prevent accidental escalation and manage risks associated with military and foundational technologies. The ambassador said the fragmented and dispersed nature of emerging technologies required layered governance frameworks, accountability measures and, where appropriate, legally binding instruments. “Delaying regulation to secure advantage and domination will not work,” he cautioned, adding that discriminatory agendas and forums with selective representation would not help address the challenges. Pakistan believes discussions on the development and deployment of emerging technologies, particularly their implications for arms control, should take place in inclusive and representative multilateral forums under UN auspices. While supporting the Security Council’s engagement with emerging technologies, Shah said its discussions should focus on their operational implications, including the implementation of Council mandates in peacekeeping, peacebuilding and conflict resolution. He also highlighted the potential of artificial intelligence and unmanned aerial vehicles to improve civilian protection and the safety and security of UN peacekeepers. The country’s envoy added that the use of new technologies, particularly UAVs and AI, by terrorist groups and other non-state actors could also be addressed in the renewal of Security Council mandates.

items.title: Mamprugu Moagduri Assembly empowers 76 persons with disabilities, introduces ‘Differently Able’ label
items.description: The Mamprugu Moagduri District Assembly has empowered 76 persons living with disabilities with various items and financial support to improve their livelihoods, expand their businesses and support their education. The beneficiaries received items including deep freezers, sewing machines, wheelchairs and laptops, alongside cash support for business development, at a short ceremony held at the forecourt of the Assembly premises. The Assembly also says it is adopting the term “Differently Able” in place of Persons Living with Disabilities, arguing that the new description is more positive and empowering. The District Coordinating Director, Issahaku Yakubu, speaking on behalf of the District Chief Executive, said the intervention was made possible through the District Assembly’s share of the Disability Common Fund. He explained that the support was intended to help beneficiaries engage in productive economic activities, improve their mobility and meet educational needs. He urged beneficiaries to use the items for their intended purposes, stressing that the Assembly would introduce a monitoring system to assess how the support was being utilised. According to him, the Assembly intends to strengthen its follow-up mechanisms, including providing training to ensure beneficiaries derive maximum benefit from the intervention. The District Chief Executive, Abdul Rahman Abdul Aziz, said the number of beneficiaries had increased significantly over the past year, although limited resources meant the Assembly could not support everyone who applied. He disclosed that the latest disbursement covered the first and second quarters of the Disability Common Fund. The items distributed included 12 deep freezers, 18 sewing machines, three laptops, two wheelchairs and cash support for 31 beneficiaries to strengthen their businesses. Additionally, 10 students received educational assistance. The Director of Social Welfare and Community Development, Abileo Anabieli, said the Assembly received more than 170 applications but selected 76 beneficiaries after an assessment by a committee. He explained that the selection process involved verifying applicants’ needs and assessing whether the requested items could be effectively utilised in their communities. Some applicants who requested deep freezers, for instance, were redirected to alternative forms of support after assessments established that their communities lacked electricity. Mr Anabieli said the intervention was particularly important to him, having worked in the district for 14 years and witnessed the challenges confronting persons with disabilities. He assured beneficiaries that the department would conduct periodic monitoring to assess the utilisation of the items. He warned that the Assembly could consider retrieving items from beneficiaries who misuse or sell them shortly after receiving the support and reallocating them to others who could put them to productive use. One of the beneficiaries, Fatawu Adam from Jadema, expressed gratitude to the Assembly after receiving a deep freezer to support his small business. He pledged to use the equipment for its intended purpose and appealed to other beneficiaries to exercise patience while awaiting their turn for assistance. He also encouraged fellow beneficiaries to make good use of the items to improve their economic circumstances. The Assembly says the intervention forms part of efforts to promote economic independence, improve access to education and enhance the living conditions of persons with disabilities across the district.

À travers ce mot d’ordre lancé par l’Union des journalistes centrafricains (UJCA), les professionnels des médias entendent dénoncer les menaces et les intimidations dont ils sont victimes dans l’exercice de leur métier. L’organisation s’inquiète notamment des récentes pressions exercées contre les journalistes de Radio Ndeke Luka. Elle déplore une dégradation du climat de travail et appelle les autorités à garantir la sécurité des professionnels des médias et à préserver la liberté de la presse dans le pays.

items.title: World: Aucune arme, technologie ou méthode de guerre ne doit permettre que la conduite des hostilités échappe au contrôle humain, selon la présidente du CICR
items.description: Country: World Source: International Committee of the Red Cross Discours de la présidente du CICR, Mirjana Spoljaric, prononcé à l’occasion du débat public de haut niveau du Conseil de sécurité de l’Organisation des Nations Unies sur le thème « Maintien de la paix et de la sécurité internationales : le règlement des conflits à l’ère de l’évolution rapide des technologies ». Monsieur le Président, Je remercie la Lettonie d’avoir organisé cette importante réunion et de me donner l’occasion de m’exprimer devant ce Conseil. Depuis que la guerre existe, les êtres humains n’ont cessé d’inventer de nouveaux moyens de s’entretuer. Mais aujourd’hui, pour la première fois de notre histoire, nous approchons à grands pas d’un point de bascule où le sort de vies humaines pourrait être entièrement confié à des machines. L’intelligence artificielle (IA) ne se fixera pas de limites dans la conduite de la guerre. C’est aux États de les lui imposer. Au mois d’août, le Secrétaire général de l’ONU et moi-même avons réitéré notre avertissement sur les dangers que représentent les systèmes d’armes autonomes et sur les enjeux éthiques et juridiques qui leur sont liés. La semaine dernière, après des années de discussions, les États se sont réunis à Genève pour décider s’ils souhaitaient ouvrir des négociations pour établir des règles juridiquement contraignantes encadrant ces types d’armes. La septième Conférence d’examen de la Convention sur certaines armes classiques s’est achevée sans un mandat de négociation clair et immédiat. Mais les États doivent veiller à ne pas verser dans la complaisance. Les technologies évoluent à un rythme effréné sans qu’il y ait de consensus sur la manière dont elles peuvent être utilisées dans les conflits armés. Il est extrêmement dangereux d’attendre, ces capacités risquant de devenir si puissantes, répandues et enracinées qu’un véritable contrôle ne serait plus possible. Les États doivent prendre sans tarder des mesures pour que les humains, et non les machines, demeurent responsables des décisions prises en temps de guerre. Les armes autonomes qui sont conçues pour cibler des êtres humains, ou dont les effets sont imprévisibles, doivent être bannies. En adoptant et en mettant en œuvre des instruments juridiquement contraignants pour interdire ou réglementer l’utilisation de certains types d’armes frappant sans discrimination, les États ont pu par le passé et pourront à l’avenir réduire la brutalité des guerres et améliorer la sécurité de leur population. Monsieur le Président, Les guerres pilotées par l’IA n’apportent pas automatiquement des améliorations pour les civils. Bien que les militaires et les entreprises technologiques assurent que l’IA rendra la guerre plus précise et moins létale pour les civils, c’est tout le contraire que nous observons sur le terrain. Nous constatons que l’IA a d’ores et déjà pour effet d’accélérer et d’amplifier les opérations militaires, avec des conséquences dévastatrices pour les civils. Concrètement, cela peut se traduire par des centaines d’attaques se succédant à une cadence élevée, souvent sans tenir compte de leurs effets cumulés. Un tel volume et une telle succession d’attaques peuvent entraîner une catastrophe humanitaire, débordant la capacité des premiers intervenants, des organisations humanitaires et des communautés à faire face aux conséquences. Les civils ont besoin de temps pour se mettre à l’abri ou évacuer les lieux. Les hôpitaux ont besoin de temps pour reconstituer leurs stocks de fournitures. Et les équipes de réparation ont besoin de temps pour rétablir les services essentiels. Les faits démontrent par ailleurs que les systèmes d’aide à la décision fondés sur l’IA ne saisissent pas la complexité et l’imprévisibilité des champs de bataille. Ils ne parviennent pas à anticiper tous les comportements et les déplacements des civils lorsque ceux-ci cherchent à se mettre en sécurité. C’est pourquoi, quelle que soit la rigueur avec laquelle un système applique le droit international humanitaire (DIH), un jugement humain demeure indispensable pour évaluer chaque attaque. Les systèmes d’aide à la décision fondés sur l’IA peuvent en outre générer des décisions de ciblage en masse qui violent le DIH. Lorsque les modèles d’IA sont programmés sur la base d’interprétations permissives des règles de la guerre, ils se transforment en systèmes de mort et de destruction. L’IA ne peut pas remédier aux interprétations de plus en plus souples qui sont faites des règles de la guerre, pas plus qu’elle ne peut être tenue pour responsable des décisions qu’elle facilite. La responsabilité d’interpréter et d’appliquer le DIH de bonne foi revient – et doit toujours revenir – aux humains. On ne peut pas simplement « coder le DIH dans l’IA » pour remplacer l’intervention humaine. Cela ne veut pas dire pour autant que les systèmes d’IA n’aient aucun rôle à jouer, ni que leur utilisation à des fins militaires devrait être complètement interdite. Ce que nous demandons, c’est que ces systèmes renforcent le respect du DIH – plutôt que de l’affaiblir. Les systèmes fondés sur l’IA peuvent être entraînés pour promouvoir une application rigoureuse des règles et principes du DIH. Nous suggérons par exemple d’utiliser l’IA dans le domaine militaire pour cartographier les infrastructures essentielles et les habitudes des civils afin de réduire au minimum les dommages causés. L’IA pourrait ainsi contribuer à identifier des itinéraires d’évacuation pour permettre aux familles de fuir les combats en toute sécurité. Pour l’instant, toutefois, les applications de ce type ne bénéficient pas des ressources et des investissements qu’elles devraient recevoir. Les entreprises technologiques qui mettent au point et conçoivent des outils d’IA portent également une responsabilité importante. Au-delà de créer de nouvelles capacités militaires, elles dessinent les contours des guerres de demain. C’est pourquoi nous dialoguons avec elles sur la manière dont leurs outils peuvent être utilisés pour renforcer la protection des civils, dans le respect du DIH. Tout comme les États, les entreprises technologiques ont le pouvoir de rendre les champs de bataille plus sûrs ou plus dangereux pour les civils. Monsieur le Président, Réfléchissons un instant aux effets de la convergence des technologies qui façonneront les guerres du futur. Nous voyons déjà les graves conséquences que les cyberopérations fondées sur l’IA peuvent avoir en situation de paix ou dans le contexte d’activités criminelles. Imaginez maintenant les ravages occasionnés si des agents d’IA recevaient l’ordre de mener des cyberopérations contre des services essentiels en période de conflit armé. Ou s’ils devenaient incontrôlables et pouvaient attaquer des infrastructures essentielles parce que trop peu de précautions ont été prises pour limiter leur fonctionnement et protéger les réseaux civils. Nous constatons déjà l’utilisation de drones pour cibler des infrastructures essentielles. Imaginez donc les conséquences si des drones équipés d’IA sélectionnaient et attaquaient des cibles sans contrôle humain. Aucune arme, technologie ou méthode de guerre ne doit permettre que la conduite des hostilités échappe au contrôle humain. Le 7 décembre prochain, les dirigeants du monde entier se réuniront en Jordanie pour réaffirmer leur attachement aux règles de la guerre à l’occasion de la Conférence de haut niveau sur l’humanité dans la guerre. Alors que les conflits armés ne cessent d’évoluer, l’engagement politique est essentiel pour faire en sorte que le DIH protège les personnes touchées par la guerre non seulement aujourd’hui, mais aussi demain. Monsieur le Président, Je tiens à souligner que le Comité international de la Croix-Rouge ne demande pas l’arrêt de toutes les applications militaires de l’IA. Ce que nous demandons aux États, c’est d’établir des règles et des cadres internationaux clairs pour régir leur mise au point et leur utilisation. Car sans réglementation, ces technologies continueront d’être testées sur le champ de bataille, et ce sont les civils qui paieront le prix fort de ces expérimentations. La technologie doit être au service de l’humanité – et non la détruire. Je vous remercie de votre attention.

items.title: World: Presidenta del CICR: Ningún arma, tecnología ni método de guerra debería poner la conducción de las hostilidades más allá de los límites del control humano
items.description: Country: World Source: International Committee of the Red Cross Mirjana Spoljaric, presidenta del CICR, hizo la siguiente declaración durante el Debate abierto del Consejo de Seguridad de las Naciones Unidas sobre la resolución de conflictos en una era de cambio tecnológico acelerado en el marco del mantenimiento de la paz y de la seguridad internacionales Señor Presidente: Quiero expresar mi agradecimiento a Letonia por haber convocado esta importante reunión y por darme la oportunidad de dirigirme a este Consejo. Desde que existe la guerra, las personas han buscado formas innovadoras de matarse entre sí. Hoy, sin embargo, por primera vez en la historia, nos acercamos vertiginosamente a un momento en el que la vida o la muerte de los seres humanos podría quedar enteramente en manos de las máquinas. La inteligencia artificial no se impondrá sus propios límites en la guerra; tienen que hacerlo los Estados. En agosto, el Secretario General de las Naciones Unidas y yo renovamos nuestra advertencia sobre los peligros que acarrean los sistemas de armas autónomos y los límites morales y jurídicos que representan. La semana pasada, luego de años de debates, los Estados se reunieron en Ginebra para decidir si negociarían normas jurídicamente vinculantes sobre los sistemas de armas autónomos. La VII Conferencia de Examen de la Convención sobre Ciertas Armas Convencionales concluyó sin un mandato de negociación claro e inmediato. Pero los Estados no deben resignarse a la complacencia. La tecnología avanza a gran velocidad sin que haya un consenso sobre cómo se la puede aplicar en la guerra. Es extremadamente peligroso esperar hasta que estas capacidades estén tan difundidas y afianzadas o sean tan poderosas que sea imposible ejercer un control significativo. Los Estados deben actuar con urgencia para garantizar que los seres humanos, y no las máquinas, sigan siendo responsables por las decisiones que se toman en la guerra. Las armas autónomas diseñadas para atacar a seres humanos o cuyos efectos son impredecibles tienen que estar prohibidas. Adoptando e implementando instrumentos jurídicamente vinculantes que prohíban o regulen las armas indiscriminadas, los Estados tienen la capacidad de limitar la brutalidad de la guerra y de fortalecer la seguridad y la protección de su propia población. Señor Presidente: La guerra apoyada en la IA no equivale automáticamente a mejores resultados para las personas civiles. Por mucho que las fuerzas armadas y las empresas tecnológicas aseguren que la inteligencia artificial hará la guerra más precisa y menos mortífera para la población civil, lo que se manifiesta es la tendencia opuesta. Ya estamos viendo que la IA acelera y amplifica las operaciones militares, con costos desastrosos para las personas civiles. En concreto, eso puede significar cientos de ataques que se producen uno detrás del otro, a menudo sin consideración por sus efectos acumulados. Ese volumen elevado de ataques sucesivos puede provocar un desastre humanitario por exceder la capacidad de los equipos de emergencia, las organizaciones de ayuda y las comunidades para absorber las consecuencias. La población civil necesita tiempo para buscar refugio y evacuar la zona. Los hospitales necesitan tiempo para reabastecerse de insumos. Los servicios de reparación necesitan tiempo para restablecer los servicios esenciales. La evidencia demuestra también que los sistemas de apoyo a la toma de decisiones con inteligencia artificial no captan cuán complejo e impredecible es el campo de batalla. No son capaces de prever todos los modos de actuar y de moverse de las personas civiles que intentan ponerse a resguardo. Por eso, por mucho que un sistema aplique el DIH, sigue siendo esencial que cada ataque se evalúe con criterios humanos. Además, los sistemas de apoyo a la toma de decisiones con IA pueden producir decisiones en masa sobre selección de objetivos que violen el derecho internacional humanitario. Cuando los modelos de IA se programan sobre la base de interpretaciones laxas de las leyes de la guerra, se convierten en sistemas de matanza y destrucción. La IA no puede remediar que las interpretaciones de las leyes de la guerra sean cada vez más elásticas, como tampoco puede hacerse responsable por las decisiones que facilita. Interpretar y aplicar el DIH de buena fe es y debe seguir siendo una responsabilidad humana. El derecho internacional humanitario no puede sencillamente “codificarse en la IA” como sustituto de la intervención humana. Eso no significa que los sistemas de IA no puedan hacer ningún aporte ni que deban prohibirse de plano en el uso militar. Lo que pedimos es que esos sistemas fortalezcan el respeto del DIH en lugar de debilitarlo. Los sistemas de apoyo con IA se pueden entrenar para que promuevan una aplicación rigurosa de las normas y principios del DIH. Por ejemplo, planteamos que la IA se puede emplear en el ámbito militar para trazar mapas de la infraestructura esencial y los patrones de la vida civil a fin de minimizar los daños. También podría identificar las rutas de evacuación para que las familias escapen por vías seguras. Sin embargo, hoy no se están asignando recursos e inversión a esas aplicaciones en la escala debida. A las empresas de tecnología que desarrollan y diseñan inteligencia artificial también les cabe una responsabilidad considerable. No solo crean nuevas capacidades militares: están configurando el futuro de la guerra. Por eso dialogamos con ellas sobre cómo se pueden utilizar sus herramientas en cumplimiento del DIH y para mejorar la protección de las personas civiles. Las empresas de tecnología, al igual que los Estados, tienen en sus manos la posibilidad de hacer el campo de batalla más seguro o más peligroso para la población civil. Señor Presidente: Considere qué ocurre cuando convergen las tecnologías que determinan la siguiente frontera de la guerra. Ya estamos viendo las significativas consecuencias que pueden tener las ciberoperaciones apoyadas en IA en entornos donde no hay un conflicto armado en curso o en las actividades delictivas. Imagine ahora la devastación que sobrevendría si se instruyera a agentes de IA que lleven a cabo ciberoperaciones contra los servicios esenciales en contextos de conflicto armado. O si “se salieran de control” y atacaran infraestructura esencial porque no se tomaron suficientes precauciones para limitar sus operaciones y preservar las redes civiles. Ya estamos viendo que se usan drones para atacar infraestructura esencial. Imagine ahora qué pasaría si hubiera drones que utilizan la IA para seleccionar objetivos y dirigir ataques sin control humano. Ningún arma, tecnología ni método de guerra debería poner la conducción de las hostilidades más allá de los límites del control humano. El 7 de diciembre, los líderes se reunirán en Jordania con motivo de la Conferencia de alto nivel sobre la humanidad en la guerra para defender las leyes de la guerra. Los métodos de guerra evolucionan continuamente, y el compromiso político es crucial para que el DIH proteja a las personas afectadas por la guerra no solo hoy, sino también mañana. Señor Presidente: Quiero ser clara: el Comité Internacional de la Cruz Roja no llama a detener todas las aplicaciones militares de la inteligencia artificial, sino que insta a los Estados a establecer marcos y normas internacionales claros que regulen su desarrollo y su uso. Porque sin regulación, esta tecnología se seguirá probando en el campo de batalla, y las personas civiles sufrirán las consecuencias de esos ensayos y errores. La tecnología debe servir a la humanidad, no destruirla. Muchas gracias.

GTEC right to freeze PhD accreditations, but acted too late – Eduwatch
items.description: The Executive Director of Africa Education Watch (Eduwatch), Kofi Asare, has endorsed the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission’s (GTEC) decision to suspend the processing of fresh accreditation applications for PhD programmes, describing it as a necessary intervention to protect standards in doctoral education. He said the regulator was right to act to prevent further deterioration in the quality of PhD training but questioned why the intervention had come at a time when several universities had already completed their admissions processes and some students had started their programmes. Speaking on PM Express on JoyNews on Tuesday, November 24, during a discussion on the quality of doctoral programmes in Ghana, Mr Asare said the commission deserved support for taking steps to address concerns about standards, even if the action had come later than necessary. “I think that, well, the intervention is a necessary quality assurance strategy, and so it is welcome. It is better to intervene, even if much later, than not intervening at all and watching quality being compromised,” he said. He said his concern was not with the objective of the freeze but with the timing, arguing that a more proactive regulatory approach could have prevented institutions from reaching a point where students had already been admitted before questions were raised about programme quality. “At present, almost every institution I know has completed their PhD applications. They have given admission, and some have started already,” he said. Mr Asare argued that GTEC’s responsibility should not be limited to conducting audits, identifying breaches and sanctioning institutions after violations had occurred. Rather, he said, effective regulation required continuous engagement with universities, early monitoring and guidance to ensure that institutions met accreditation requirements before admitting students. He said a regulator should put systems in place to help institutions comply with quality standards and prevent violations, rather than wait until problems have emerged before taking action. According to him, the timing of regulatory interventions was particularly important in higher education because students could become caught up in disputes or institutional failures over which they had little control. “When non-compliance happens and we get to where we are, then sometimes students also panic, for they are actually, quote unquote, punished for the lapses of institutions — something that you may not be able to hold them accountable for,” he said. Mr Asare therefore called for stronger preventive oversight by GTEC to ensure that universities received timely guidance and that students were not exposed to uncertainty arising from weaknesses in institutional compliance. GTEC has said its review of PhD programmes is intended to establish whether universities have the academic staff, research facilities, supervision capacity and other resources required to deliver quality doctoral education. The commission’s suspension applies to the processing of fresh accreditation applications for PhD programmes. It is not a blanket ban on admissions into all existing, accredited doctoral programmes. The debate over the exercise has centred not only on the need to strengthen standards but also on how the regulator can manage the process without disrupting students who have already secured admission or begun their studies.

items.title: WHO Director-General announces support for vaccines, medical equipment during official visit to Cuba
items.description: Country: Cuba Source: World Health Organization Today, World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced US$2 million to help strengthen Cuba’s national immunization activities and provided essential medical equipment to health facilities. Dr Tedros arrived in Cuba on 22 November at the invitation of Cuba’s Minister of Public Health, Dr José Ángel Portal Miranda. During his visit, Dr Tedros toured health facilities and met with President Miguel Díaz-Canel Bermúdez. He was joined by senior officials from WHO and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). WHO’s new funding will support Cuban health sector priorities, with a focus on the National Immunization Program, especially vaccination for children and adults. Cuba has maintained very high vaccination coverage, of above 98%, for many years. In 2025, coverage decreased to 95%. WHO’s contribution will support immunization for approximately 62 000 newborns, more than 780 000 girls and boys, and over 110 000 people in other risk groups, as well as support rabies prevention and control actions. “Cuba’s hard-won public health achievements must be protected,” said Dr Tedros. “WHO/PAHO’s provision of essential vaccines is the latest demonstration of our commitment to support Cuba through significant health challenges and help maintain access to essential health services. Together with our partners, we will continue to stand with the Cuban people to protect health, save lives and sustain progress.” During his visit, Dr Tedros reaffirmed WHO/PAHO’s continuing support for the country's health services, and ways to protect progress in public health. Strengthening health cooperation was a central topic of Dr Tedros’s visit to Cuba. Between 2025 and 2026, WHO and PAHO have mobilized more than US$14 million through 14 projects to support the quality and sustainability of health services and strengthen health workforce capacities. During his mission, Dr Tedros visited the "William Soler" University Pediatric Hospital and the pediatric cardiocenter of the same name, meeting health workers and families of children receiving care there. The delegation delivered supplies and medical equipment mobilized with the support of the PAHO/WHO Emergency team, including basic medical care kits and equipment to strengthen the institution's response capacity: electronic monitors for blood pressure measurement; ophthalmoscopes/otoscopes, pulse oximeters, sphygmomanometers, stethoscopes, thermometers, among other resources. Dr Tedros also held discussions with the United Nations Country Team and other cooperation partners in Cuba on sustaining financial and strategic support for the country’s public health sector. These meetings identified new opportunities to expand collaboration and coordination according to the country's main health needs. The WHO Director-General was also updated by executives from Cuba’s main biotechnology companies on advances and challenges to the country’s pharmaceutical industry, which are developing new products in the areas of infectious disease prevention and control, Alzheimer's, cancer, and diabetes. This was Dr Tedros’s second official visit to Cuba as WHO Director-General. His previous visit took place in 2018. On this trip, Dr Tedros was accompanied by Raúl Thomas, WHO’s Assistant Director-General of Business Operations, and Dr Ciro Ugarte, Director of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Health Emergencies Department. Dr Tedros will visit other countries in the region this week. About WHO Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. “Together for health. Stand with science”, the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide. items.title: IDS Working Paper 631: Countering Backlash through Coalition Building: Compromises, Contentions, and Sustaining Struggles in Bangladesh
items.description: Country: Bangladesh Source: Institute of Development Studies Bangladesh has made impressive progress in promoting gender equality, but recent backlash from state and non-state actors against these gains has led women’s rights and feminist groups to form coalitions in response. This study focuses on four different coalitions formed around different demands – decent wages, child marriage prevention, comprehensive sexuality education, and rape law reform – to examine how feminist coalitions in Bangladesh respond to intensifying backlash against hard won gains. It finds that coalition building is important but unevenly effective against different forms of backlash. The selected coalitions had successfully expanded public legitimacy for feminist causes and influenced discourse, but were less able to counter state repression, co-option of feminist agendas by the regime, and structural inequalities. Strategic framing by coalitions enabled access to policy spaces but often required compromising transformative agendas, particularly on sexuality and LGBTQI rights. The findings highlight both the value and the limits of coalition strategies in restrictive and transitional contexts. Access this publication Read full publication online in OpenDocs

items.title: “We’ve lost a titan, legend, an icon,” Gov Mbah mourns Pete Edochie
items.description: Governor of Enugu State, Dr. Peter Mbah, has expressed deep grief over the passing on of one of Nollywood’s greatest, Chief Pete Edochie, describing it as the departure of a giant, icon, and patriot. Mbah further described it as a personal loss to Enugu State, recalling that although the renown thespian hailed from Nteje in Anambra State, he had unequivocally acknowledged his life-long ties with Enugu State, which he had often described as his birth place, his “first port of call,” and a home away from home. The Governor, in his personal tribute to Edochie in the early hours of Wednesday, following the announcement of the actor’s demise, aged 79, by his son, Leo Pete Edochie, further explained that the deceased was a great ambassador of Enugu State and fan of his administration. “I am deeply saddened by the passing of Chief Pete Edochie, one of Nigeria’s most iconic actors and titans, and one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood and Africa’s creative industry across the world. “The pain of this loss is further deepened by its timing. It comes at a particularly poignant moment when Enugu, a city whose history and identity are deeply intertwined with the arts, is hosting the National Festival of Arts and Culture (NAFEST). “At a time when we are celebrating the richness of our cultural heritage and the creative talents that give it expression, we are confronted with the loss of one of its most distinguished ambassadors. It is a sobering reminder that while we celebrate the enduring power of our arts and culture, we must also mourn those who gave them life and brought them global recognition. “Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor; he was an institution. With his commanding screen presence, unmistakable voice, remarkable mastery of dialogue and profound understanding of his craft, he helped shape the identity of Nigerian cinema and took the stories, values and cultural expressions of our people to audiences across the world. As an illustrious son of the South East, and dating back to his role as a tragic protagonist in the dramatization of Chinua Achebe’s 1958 novel, ‘Things Fall Apart,’ Edochie eloquently interpreted the society to the world. He wore his Igbo identity with pride, bringing its language, wisdom, proverbs and rich cultural heritage to life in ways that resonated far beyond our shores. “His performances transcended entertainment, preserving aspects of our cultural heritage and inspiring generations of actors and storytellers. “His was a career defined not merely by longevity but by excellence, distinction and enduring influence and uncommon social grace. “Even as the curtain falls on this remarkable life, his legacy as a fine broadcaster, thespian, cultural ambassador, and super star will continue to live on in the countless lives he touched and the generations of performers he inspired. “Although this is a personal loss to us as Ndi Enugu, my heart, nevertheless, particularly goes out to his immediate household. On behalf of the Government and people of Enugu State, I extend my heartfelt condolences to his family, the Nollywood community, the Government and people of Anambra State, and all Nigerians and his global fans, who mourn this monumental loss. May God grant his family the strength to bear this irreparable loss and grant his gentle soul eternal rest. Adieu, Chief Pete Edochie, MON. Adieu Ononenyi, Ebubedike, Gaga n’ ogwu, Ogadagidi, Nwoke ka Ibe Ya, Okara Mmadu Okara Mmuo, a legend, fine gentleman, veteran broadcaster and actor. “Your voice may have gone silent, but your legacy will speak for generations,” the governor mourned. items.title: World: ICRC president: No weapon, technology or method of war should put the conduct of hostilities beyond the limits of human control [EN/AR]
items.description: Country: World Source: International Committee of the Red Cross Please refer to the attached file. The following statement was delivered by ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric at the UN Security Council High-Level Open Debate on the “Maintenance of International Peace and Security: Conflict Resolution in an Era of Rapid Technological Change.” Mr President, Thank you to Latvia for convening this important meeting and giving me the opportunity to brief this Council. For as long as there has been war, people have found new ways to kill each other. But today, for the first time in history, we are rapidly approaching a moment where human lives may be entirely surrendered to machines. AI will not set its own limits in warfare. States must. In August, the UN Secretary General and I renewed our warning about the dangers autonomous weapons systems pose and the moral and legal red lines they represent. Last week, after years of discussions, States gathered in Geneva to decide if they would negotiate legally binding rules on autonomous weapons systems. The Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded without a clear and immediate negotiation mandate. But States must not resign themselves to complacency. Technology is advancing at high speed without a shared understanding of how it can be applied in war. It is extremely dangerous to wait until these capabilities are so widespread, entrenched or powerful that meaningful control is no longer possible. States must take urgent action to ensure that humans, and not machines, remain accountable for decisions in war. Autonomous weapons that are designed to target humans, or whose effects are unpredictable, must be prohibited. By adopting and implementing legally binding instruments that prohibit or regulate indiscriminate types of weapons, States have been able to and can still limit the brutality of war and enhance the safety and security of their own people. Mr President, AI-powered warfare does not automatically equal better outcomes for civilians. Despite assurances from militaries and technology companies that AI will make warfare more precise and less lethal for civilians, we are witnessing opposite trends. We are seeing AI already accelerating and amplifying military operations, with disastrous costs to civilians. In real-world terms, this can mean hundreds of attacks carried out in rapid-fire succession, often without consideration for their cumulative effects. The high volume and sequencing of attacks can trigger a humanitarian disaster by outstripping the capacity for first responders, aid organisations, and communities to absorb the consequences. Civilians need time to shelter and evacuate. Hospitals need time to replenish supplies. Repair services need time to restore essential services. Evidence also shows that AI decision-support systems do not capture the complexity and unpredictability of the battlefield. They cannot anticipate all the ways in which civilians behave and move when they are seeking safety. That is why, no matter how faithfully a system applies IHL, human judgement remains essential in assessing each attack. AI decision-support systems can also mass produce targeting decisions that violate international humanitarian law. When AI models are programmed based on lax interpretations of the rules of war, they become systems of killing and destruction. AI cannot remedy increasingly elastic interpretations of the rules of war, nor can it be held accountable for the decisions it facilitates. Good-faith interpretation and application of IHL are – and must remain – a human responsibility. International humanitarian law cannot simply be “coded into AI” as a substitute for human involvement. But this does not mean that AI systems have no role to play or should be prohibited in military use altogether. What we are asking for is that these systems strengthen IHL compliance – not undermine it. AI support systems can be trained to promote a rigorous application of the rules and principles of IHL. For instance, we suggest that AI in the military domain could be used to map essential infrastructure and patterns of civilian life to minimise harm. It could identify evacuation routes for families to escape safely. However, today, resourcing and investment are not being directed towards these applications at the scale they should be. Technology companies developing and designing AI also bear significant responsibility. They are not simply creating new military capabilities; they are shaping the future of warfare. That is why we engage with them on how their tools can be used in compliance with IHL and to enhance civilian protection. Technology companies, like States, have the power to make the battlefield safer or more dangerous for civilians. Mr President, Consider what happens when the technologies shaping the next frontier of warfare converge. We already see the significant consequences that AI-enabled cyber operations can have in non-conflict settings or in criminal activities. Now imagine the devastation if AI agents are instructed to conduct cyber operations against essential services in armed conflict. Or if they “go rogue” and attack essential infrastructure because insufficient precautions have been taken to limit their operations and protect civilian networks. We already see how drones are used to target essential infrastructure. Now imagine the consequences if AI-enabled drones select and engage targets without human control. No weapon, technology or method of war should put the conduct of hostilities beyond the limits of human control. On 7 December, leaders will gather in Jordan at the High-Level Humanity in War Conference to stand behind the rules of war. As warfare evolves, political commitment is critical to ensuring that IHL protects people living through war not only today, but tomorrow. Mr President, Let me be clear: the International Committee of the Red Cross is not calling for all military applications of AI to stop. We are calling on States to establish clear international frameworks and rules that regulate their development and use. Because without regulations, this technology will continue to be tested on the battlefield, and civilians will be subjected to the consequences of trial and error. Technology must serve humanity and not destroy it. Thank you.

items.title: Thieves steal 49,000 litres of fuel from PSO pipeline in Islamabad
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Thieves have stolen 49,000 litres of fuel worth Rs17.6 million from the main Pakistan State Oil (PSO) pipeline laid in the capital’s rural area since October 16. Following a complaint lodged by Mohammad Rahmet Ullah, an official at the PSO Sihala Terminal, police registered a case under Sections 462-B (tampering with petroleum pipelines) and 34 (acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code. According to the FIR, the PSO Sihala installations are connected to Attock Refinery Limited via a 15-kilometre-long, eight-inch-diameter pipeline. Since October 16, officials have noticed a continuous drop in pipeline pressure during specific hours each day, prompting strict surveillance of the line to track down the oil theft. PSO security guards, while patrolling the pipeline, observed suspicious activity involving a Shahzore truck equipped with a tank at a house in Model Town on Nov 23. The matter was brought to the knowledge of the area police. Later, the police, accompanied by a PSO security team, reached the house and found a man there. The house was searched, leading to the discovery of a truck, a Bolan vehicle and a motorcycle. Upon further inquiry and based on information provided by the man, a pit was discovered beneath a floor slab in the house’s kitchen. A high-pressure pipe and a nozzle were found installed in the pit for the purpose of stealing oil. The man further revealed that the pipeline runs along the wall, extending towards a plot. Acting on the information, the floor of the sitting room was dug, revealing a tunnel underneath. According to the man, it connected directly to the main pipeline of the PSO. During investigation, the man revealed that in collusion with his accomplices, he had long been involved in stealing petroleum products from various locations and at different times. The complainant said the accused caused a loss of approximately 49,000 litres of diesel worth Rs17.6 million to PSO. In October 2024, thieves stole 302,046 litres of diesel worth over Rs80 million from a PSO pipeline laid in the area of Humak in a similar way. In July 2026, the Federal Investigation Agency, in a joint operation with PSO, busted a network involved in stealing diesel from PSO’s main pipeline near Sihala and arrested two suspects. The network reportedly operated for five to six months, and 20,000 litres of diesel were being illegally extracted from the pipeline daily. Published in Dawn, November 25th, 2026

items.title: “Water comes before roads”: PURC boss urges government to replicate Big Push agenda in water sector
items.description: The Executive Secretary of the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission (PURC), Dr Shafic Suleman, has made an impassioned case for a major national investment in Ghana’s water sector, declaring that “water comes before roads” as he toured Ghana Water Limited (GWL) facilities in the Bono East Region. Speaking during a working tour of utility operations, Dr Suleman urged the Mahama-led administration to replicate its ambitious “Big Push” agenda in the road sector within the water sector, arguing that access to potable water deserves equal—if not greater—national priority. “I am urging the government to make a bold move by replicating its Big Push agenda in the road sector to the water sector. We need a big push in water because water comes before roads,” Dr Suleman said. His call comes amid mounting concerns over the impact of galamsey (illegal mining) on Ghana’s water bodies and the urgent need to bridge supply gaps across the country. Techiman shines as a model of river protection Inspecting the Tanoso Water Treatment Plant in the Techiman Municipality, Dr Suleman was full of praise for local efforts to protect the Tano River. Visibly impressed by the clean nature of the water, he commended authorities in the Techiman area for preserving the sanctity of the river, which is traditionally revered as a sacred deity. “I am truly impressed by the clean nature of the water here. The authorities in the Techiman area deserve commendation for their efforts in protecting the sanctity of the Tano River, with its traditional belief that the river is a sacred god that deserves to be preserved,” he said. “It is my wish that other regions emulate this same example.” His words carry particular weight as galamsey continues to threaten rivers nationwide. GWL Bono Ahafo Regional Chief Manager, Ing. Theophilus Tawiah Collins, briefed the team on baseline expansion studies and ongoing discussions on suspended projects. He called on all stakeholders to rally behind Ghana Water Limited in its mission to deliver potable water supply across the country. “I call on all to support Ghana Water Limited in its efforts to ensure potable water supply across the country,” Ing. Collins urged. Tanoso plant impresses The team also assessed the Tanoso Water Treatment Plant, recognised as one of the cleanest water sources in the country. The tour included the Bono East Regional Manager of the PURC, Cassiel Eghan Asiedu, along with other regional and national staff of the Commission. A broader mission The tour forms part of the PURC’s ongoing efforts to address galamsey pollution, water quality, and supply gaps—ensuring that consumers across Ghana have access to safe, reliable, and affordable water services.

items.title: Paris Club Refunds: ‘We have no hands in transaction’ – Nigeria Governors’ Forum
items.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA – THE Nigeria Governors’ Forum, the umbrella body of the 36 state governors has denied having transactions with regard to the N135.5 billion paid to the forum as stakeholder in the Paris Club refunds dispute. Read Also: Paris Club Refunds: Court freezes N135.5bn linked to Governors’ Forum The NGF said it did not engage any party thereto, nor held any such monies in its custody at any time. The governors made the clarification in a statement signed very late yesterday night by Director Media and Strategic Communications NGF, Yunusa Tanko Abdullahi. It was in reaction to reports on the Federal Capital Territory Court interim order freezing N135.5 billion linked to Governors’ Forum and restraining 29 banks. The Forum said: “The Nigeria Governors’ Forum (NGF) is aware of recent media reports regarding the November 19, 2026 interim order, obtained exparte, issued by the Federal High Court of the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Abuja in the Paris Club refund suit filed by Dr. Ted Iseghohi-Edwards from events that happened in 2016. “Please note that this issue emanated from allegations of transactions between the plaintiff and the Association of Local Government of Nigeria, ALGON. The Nigeria Governors Forum has no hand in that transaction and did not engage any party thereto, nor held any such monies in its custody at any time. “Meanwhile, the NGF’s legal team is currently reviewing the court processes and will respond accordingly. The Forum reiterates its unwavering commitment to the rule of law, transparency and accountability.” Abuja High Court order Justice O. C. Agbaza granted the interim Mareva injunction following an ex-parte application brought by Dr. Ted Iseghohi-Edwards. The order restrained the Incorporated Trustees of the NGF from withdrawing, transferring, dissipating or otherwise dealing with the funds. The order also restrained 29 commercial banks from releasing, transferring, converting or otherwise dealing with funds belonging to the NGF within their custody. The judge further directed the banks to disclose, within 48 hours of service, whether the NGF maintains accounts containing the disputed funds. The banks are required to identify such accounts, their currencies, available balances and amounts preserved under the court’s order. The amount represents 100 million dollar, equivalent to the N135.55 billion, calculated at the exchange rate of N1,355.80 to the dollar. Justice Agbaza made the orders on November 19, following the ex parte application and submissions by the claimant’s Counsel, Emonye Adekwu, SAN, alongside Damilola Odesola, from Ade Okeaya-Inneh & Co. Law Firm. According to the report, Iseghohi-Edwards, who carries on business as Edwards and Partners Law Firm, had sought the recovery of the money pursuant to an indemnity issued by the NGF. The claimant’s case is that the money belongs to him under an indemnity dated December 20, 2018, issued by the NGF. The indemnity reportedly arose from an arrangement under which the Federal Government paid 100 million dollar to the NGF as stakeholder. The money was to be held pending the determination of the Federal Government’s liability to Iseghohi-Edwards over legal and consultancy fees, just it arose from services allegedly rendered in connection with the London and Paris Club loan transaction. Iseghohi-Edwards claimed he was retained by the Incorporated Trustees of the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria (ALGON) to represent the 774 local government councils in the London and Paris Clubs refunds matters. The first respondent in the suit is the Incorporated Trustees of the Nigerian Governors’ Forum. The 29 banks are joined as co- respondents. items.title: L’incertitude météorologique pourrait faire grimper les prix du gaz en Europe cet hiver
items.description: Selon Nicholas Klingaman, ancien directeur de la météo chez Citadel, l'hiver 2026-2027 pourrait voir un El Niño d'une puissance record interagir avec des épisodes d'oscillation de Madden-Julian (MJO) plus nombreux et plus intenses que d'ordinaire Ex-Citadel Weather Head Reveals Wild Card Tied to El Niño », Bloomberg , 22 novembre 2026.'> 1 . Une telle configuration est rare : seuls trois « super El Niño » ont été mesurés depuis 1950, dont ceux de 1997-1998 et 2015-2016, qui avaient coïncidé avec une forte activité de la MJO. La MJO est une impulsion de pluie, de vent et de nuages qui se déplace vers l'est, de l'océan Indien vers le Pacifique, tous les un à deux mois. Celle-ci revient en permanence, avec des phases plus ou moins actives, mais seulement ses épisodes les plus intenses atteignent le Pacifique. Ses ondulations atmosphériques peuvent traverser plusieurs milliers de kilomètres, ce qui modifie la circulation atmosphérique jusqu'aux latitudes moyennes. En hiver, elle influence l'oscillation nord-atlantique (ONA), qui conditionne en grande partie le temps en Europe. Selon Klingaman, la MJO pourrait compliquer les prévisions fondées sur El Niño, car ses effets ne deviennent visibles que quelques semaines à l'avance. Sa rencontre avec El Niño pourrait ainsi faire dévier les températures en Europe de ce qui est attendu, avec les écarts les plus froids entre fin janvier et mars. Selon une étude parue fin 2023 dans la revue Nature Climate Change , la prévisibilité de la MJO a augmenté au cours du XXe siècle. En hiver, les modèles météorologiques peuvent théoriquement l'anticiper environ six jours plus tôt qu'il y a 100 ans, à une quarantaine de jours d'échéance en moyenne. Le réchauffement climatique expliquerait une partie de cette hausse, qui devrait se poursuivre au XXIe siècle, en rendant la MJO plus intense et plus régulière et al. , « Increase in MJO predictability under global warming », Nature Climate Change , 2024, vol. 14, n°1, p. 68-74.'> 2 . La relation entre température et consommation de gaz en Europe est quasi linéaire. En France, en Allemagne et en Italie, le froid explique à lui seul environ 90 % des variations mensuelles de la consommation entre 2015 et 2025, selon une analyse de la revue. En septembre, Goldman Sachs avait souligné dans une analyse le poids des écarts par rapport aux normales saisonnières sur les prix du gaz en Europe cet hiver. Selon la banque américaine, en hiver, la température peut faire varier la demande de gaz de l'équivalent d'environ 12 % de la capacité de stockage Will European Gas Prices Keep Rising This Winter ? , Goldman Sachs, 23 septembre 2026.'> 3 . L'effet sur les prix est asymétrique : un hiver plus froid que la moyenne d'un écart-type ferait monter la prévision de prix moyen de l'hiver d'environ 75 %, tandis qu’un hiver plus doux d'un écart-type la ferait baisser d'environ 30 %. Les prix du gaz ont bondi en Europe en début de semaine en raison de nouvelles prévisions météorologiques qui annonçaient une vague de froid, liée cette fois à l'effondrement précoce du vortex polaire . Lundi 23, le contrat de référence a gagné jusqu'à 8,6 % en séance, à 96 euros par mégawattheure (MWh). L’article L'incertitude météorologique pourrait faire grimper les prix du gaz en Europe cet hiver est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Burundi: Humanitarian Action for Children 2026 - Protecting children amid overlapping crises in the Great Lakes, Revision 1 (November 2026)
items.description: Countries: Burundi, Rwanda, Uganda, United Republic of Tanzania Source: UN Children's Fund Please refer to the attached file. HIGHLIGHTS • In 2026, 6.1 million people, including children, will require urgent humanitarian assistance across Burundi, Rwanda, Uganda and the United Republic of Tanzania, as conflict spillover, displacement, climate shocks, malnutrition and disease outbreaks heighten risks to children’s survival, protection and well-being. • Persistent threats remain of public health outbreaks; through cross border transmission in a subregion marked by porous borders, high population mobility and fragile surveillance systems. In 2026, active Ebola transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda’s outbreak (officially declared over on 28 July), demonstrates these risks. Rising malnutrition, Cholera and other disease outbreaks are compounding risks for refugees and vulnerable host communities, where overstretched WASH, health and basic services require sustained preparedness, surveillance, regional coordination and life-saving support for children and affected communities. • UNICEF will scale up rapid, multisectoral life-saving assistance while reinforcing national systems to sustain access to essential services for both refugees and host communities. This integrated response will be anchored in community-based delivery, preparedness and early action and a coordinated cross-border response. UNICEF will work through local partners and government systems to maximize reach, timeliness and accountability. • UNICEF urgently requires $45 million to ensure more than 1.2 million children can access lifesaving treatment, safe water, protection and learning. Without sustained and flexible funding, the risks to children’s survival, well-being and rights will escalate sharply.

items.title: Humanitarian Action for Children 2026 - Colombia, Revision 1 (November 2026)
items.description: Country: Colombia Source: UN Children's Fund Please refer to the attached file. HIGHLIGHTS Colombia faces multiple, overlapping crises. Armed conflict, climate- and weather-related hazards, and challenges associated with mixed migration flows. Restricted humanitarian access further limits the delivery of assistance to the most vulnerable communities. Overall, an estimated 11.6 million people, including approximately 4.2 million children, will require humanitarian assistance in 2026. On 10 August 2026, a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicentre in San José del Palmar, Choco. UNICEF will deliver multisectoral interventions in health and nutrition, education, child protection and WASH, with an emphasis on localized and scalable approaches, promoting peacebuilding and community engagement and supporting partners and institutions to sustain impact in remote areas. UNICEF requires $53.9 million in 2026 to reach 447,473 people, including 297,049 children, with life-saving services and supplies in priority territories identified through interagency planning. This includes $27.1 million under the initial HAC, aligned with the initial HNRP, and $26.8 million under the HAC Addendum, aligned with the HNRP Addendum.
