items.title: Belarus: Europe: Judgments on ‘instrumentalization’ of migration a devastating blow to the absolute prohibition of torture
items.description: Countries: Belarus, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, World Source: Amnesty International Today, the European Court of Human Rights ruled on cases of summary forced returns at the borders of Latvia , Lithuania and Poland with Belarus, also known as pushbacks, in cases of “instrumentalization of migration” defined by the Court as the actions of a state encouraging, facilitating or forcing migration with the aim of destabilizing another state. The Court found that summary returns at the border in this context constitute a violation of the prohibition of torture only where applicants showed “evident personal vulnerabilities” or were able to demonstrate a real and immediate threat to life or risk of ill-treatment. Reacting to the judgments, Mandi Mudarikwa, Head of Strategic Litigation at Amnesty International said: “These rulings strike a devastating blow to legal certainty and the protection of human rights at the borders under the European Convention of Human Rights. They limit the absolute protections guaranteed under the Convention only to people who are able to show evident vulnerabilities or that they are at immediate risk. This is despite the Convention entrenching such rights, such as the prohibition of torture, as absolute and the Court itself recognizing this fact. “This marks a dangerous departure from the Court’s long held view that evidence requirements should not preclude individuals from protection from torture and other prohibited treatment. Any challenges facing states or even situations of ‘emergency’ cannot absolve them of their human rights obligations. “Once again, racialized migrants and refugees are being exposed to successive violations of their rights: first, subjected to abuse by Belarus, and now denied justice. This is a bleak day for refugee and migrant rights in Europe and a stark reminder of the widening gap between Europe’s human rights commitments and its actions. “But these judgments are by no means a green light for states to bypass people’s rights at the borders. As acknowledged by the Court, states are still bound by international human rights and refugee law, including the right to seek asylum. “As an intervener in two of the three cases, Amnesty International is seriously concerned by today’s ruling. We are studying the findings in full and will issue a full response in due course.” Background The three rulings concerned allegations of serious human rights violations, including unlawful pushbacks, summary returns of migrants and refugees at the border, from Latvia, Lithuania and Poland to Belarus. Amnesty International submitted third-party interventions to the Court in the cases against Lithuania and Latvia . The Court found that summary returns at the border constitute a violation of Art. 3 of the Convention (prohibition of torture) only in respect of some of the applicants in the cases of Latvia and Poland, attaching weight to applicants’ ability of either showing “evident personal vulnerabilities” or demonstrating a real and immediate threat to life or risk of ill-treatment to prevent their summary returns. The Court also found violations under the right to liberty (Art. 5) in the cases against Lithuania and Latvia. In the case of Latvia, the Court found violations of Article 3 for some of the applicants also in relation to the material conditions of the applicants’ stay while at the border. Amnesty International has long documented violence and abuses of human rights at these borders. In these EU countries, abuse of emergency powers has escalated into several human rights violations, including unlawful returns , torture and other ill-treatment , arbitrary detention , and the use of intimidation and violence to force people to return “voluntarily”.

items.title: Reading the Odds: A Ghanaian football fan’s guide to sports betting markets
items.description: Football conversation in Ghana rarely stops at the final whistle. Whether it is a Ghana Premier League derby, a Black Stars qualifier on the road to AFCON 2027 or a big Saturday in the English Premier League, fans love to debate who will win, how many goals will go in and which side will keep a clean sheet. For fans who also enjoy a bet on the action, those debates come with a set of numbers attached. Odds, markets and bet slips can look confusing at first, but the basics are simple once you know what each figure means. This guide explains how it all works. How Sports Betting Has Grown in Ghana Sports betting has become a familiar part of Ghana’s football culture, and the market is regulated. The Gaming Commission of Ghana oversees betting operators, vets their advertising, and sets the player-protection standards they must meet. The arrival of international operators has given fans more choice. Kaizen Gaming launched Betano in Ghana in February 2026, its 20th market worldwide and its second in Africa after Nigeria, with sports betting built around football and a mobile-first design. Understanding Decimal Odds Most betting sites in Ghana display odds in decimal format, the easiest to read. The number shows your total return for every cedi staked, including your stake. For example, if Hearts of Oak are priced at 2.50 to win a match and you stake GH₵10, a winning bet returns GH₵25. That is your GH₵10 stake back plus GH₵15 profit. Lower odds, such as 1.40, mean the bookmaker sees an outcome as more likely, while higher odds, such as 4.00 or above, point to a less likely result. A quick way to see what the odds imply is to divide 1 by the decimal price. Odds of 2.00 suggest roughly a 50% chance, while odds of 4.00 suggest about 25%. These figures reflect how the market views a match, making them a useful talking point before kick-off. The Most Popular Football Markets The classic market is the match result, often shown as 1X2. Here, 1 stands for a home win, X for a draw and 2 for an away win. It is the starting point for most fans, especially in a league as competitive as the Ghana Premier League, where draws are common. Double chance covers two of the three outcomes in one bet, such as a home win or a draw. Because it covers more possibilities, the odds are lower than for a straight win. Goal markets are just as popular. Over/under bets focus on the total number of goals, with lines such as over or under 2.5 goals. Both teams to score, often shortened to BTTS, asks a simple question: will each side find the net at least once? Handicap markets give one team a virtual head start or deficit to balance a lopsided fixture. If a strong side is given a minus-one handicap, it needs to win by two or more goals for the bet to succeed. Single Bets and Accumulators A single bet is a wager on one outcome. An accumulator, often called a multiple or “acca”, combines several selections on one bet slip. The odds multiply, producing a bigger potential return, but every selection must win for the bet to pay out. If one leg loses, the whole accumulator loses. Many fans enjoy building weekend accas around the Premier League and the local league, picking a handful of fixtures they have been following all week. Following the Game as It Happens Football in Ghana is a mobile experience. Fans follow scores, stats, and line-ups on their phones, and the same goes for betting. Odds move before kick-off as team news, injuries, and market opinion change, and many operators also offer in-play betting, with prices updating as the game unfolds. That makes the odds themselves part of the entertainment. Watching a price shorten after an early goal or a red card adds another layer to following a match, whether you are at the stadium or watching from home. Know Who Regulates the Market Before opening an account with any betting operator, check that it is authorised to operate in Ghana. The Gaming Commission of Ghana regulates the sector and publishes rules licensed operators must follow, including standards on advertising and player protection. Licensed operators must also verify customers’ identity and age, and betting is strictly for those aged 18 and over. Enjoying the Game Odds and markets add another dimension to the football Ghanaians already love, from local derbies to continental qualifiers and Europe’s biggest leagues. Treat betting as entertainment, set a time and spending limit before you start, and enjoy the debates as much as the results.

items.title: ‘We need quality PhDs’ – Former GES boss backs GTEC freeze
items.description: Former Director-General of the Ghana Education Service (GES), Prof Kwasi Opoku Amankwah, has thrown his weight behind the decision by the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) to suspend the processing of fresh accreditation applications for PhD programmes, saying the regulator is acting within its mandate to protect the quality of higher education. He said the move was necessary to ensure that universities had the academic capacity, infrastructure and supervision arrangements required to train doctoral students, warning that the country needed to pay closer attention to the standards of its PhD programmes. Speaking on PM Express on JoyNews on Tuesday, November 24, Prof Amankwah said he fully supported GTEC’s intervention, although he urged the commission to communicate clearly when its review was completed and the suspension lifted. “I fully support that,” he said, referring to the decision to put new PhD programme accreditations on hold. He, however, cautioned that the commission should not leave universities and the public uncertain about the duration of the exercise or whether the restrictions remained in force after the review. He said GTEC should inform stakeholders when it had completed its assessment and was ready to resume processing applications, even if it could not immediately disclose all the details of its findings. “…I hope that when they are done, at least if they don’t tell us even the details, they should tell us that they have now taken up the freeze and then they can go ahead, rather than to let this thing hang, to be like there’s a problem somewhere,” he said. Prof Amankwah said the country needed to take the quality of doctoral education seriously, adding that he had encountered PhD programmes whose standards raised concerns. He indicated that he had personal experience of assessing some programmes, although he declined to discuss the details during the interview. “We need to actually look at it. I have a story to tell, but maybe some other time, about some PhD that I looked at and all that. So we need to actually have quality PhDs, and it’s something that they should be working on,” he said. He maintained that reviewing the standards of doctoral programmes was a legitimate responsibility of the regulator and that GTEC should be allowed to carry out that duty. “I fully agree with them. It is within their mandate,” he added. GTEC has explained that its current exercise is aimed at assessing the capacity of institutions running PhD programmes, including the availability of qualified academic supervisors, research facilities and other requirements for doctoral training. The commission’s decision to pause the processing of fresh accreditation applications has generated debate among university authorities and academics, with concerns raised about the possible implications for institutions seeking approval and programmes undergoing accreditation processes. However, GTEC has clarified that the measure is not a blanket ban on admissions into all existing, accredited PhD programmes. The exercise is intended to strengthen quality assurance and ensure that institutions meet the required standards before new doctoral programmes are approved.

items.title: NHIA CEO hails students’ brilliance as Afia Kobi Ampem Girls’ SHS triumphs in Middle Belt quiz competition
items.description: Afia Kobi Ampem Girls Senior High School has won the Middle Belt edition of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) Inter-School Quiz Competition, cementing its place as one of the brightest schools in the zone. The Kumasi-based girls’ school, representing the Ashanti Region, outshone four other regional champions to lift the coveted Middle Belt trophy at the contest held at Opoku Ware School. It was a closely fought contest from the opening round to the final question, with all five schools displaying impressive knowledge of the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) and general current affairs. At the end of the contest, Afia Kobi Ampem Girls Senior High School finished top with 60 points. St Joseph SHS from Western North and Bechem Presbyterian SHS from Ahafo tied for second place with 57 points each, underscoring the competitive nature of the championship. Koase STEM Senior High Technical School from Bono placed fourth with 55 points, while Akumfi Ameyaw Senior High Technical School from Bono East came fifth with 52 points. For their outstanding performance, Afia Kobi Ampem Girls Senior High School received a cash prize of GH¢5,000, while St Joseph SHS and Bechem Presbyterian SHS each received GH¢2,500 for placing second and third respectively. All participating schools also received certificates of participation. Speaking after the contest, the Chief Executive Officer of the NHIA, Dr Victor Asare Bampoe, expressed admiration for the depth of knowledge displayed by the competing teams. According to him, he was particularly struck by the level of preparation and confidence exhibited by the students throughout the competition, describing their performance as exceptional. “At some point we were even asking ourselves, those of us who work at NHIA, would we be able to answer some of these questions? It all goes to show that the preparation has been great,” he said. He described the initiative as a good opportunity, especially at a time when the Authority is working to empower Ghanaians against illegal payments at hospitals, pledging its continuity. “These young ladies and gentlemen can serve as advocates when they go home to empower other people so that the right things are done when it comes to the National Health Insurance Scheme,” he said. He continued: “I think it is something that would be good to stay. And whether the current team is there or not, I think the utility of this and the fact that it is going to be very useful to all Ghanaians would make it something that will stay because it is a very good programme.” The programme is designed to nurture young health insurance ambassadors who will educate their peers, families, and communities on the importance of enrolling on the NHIS and renewing their membership regularly. He stressed that the competition was not just about winning prizes, but carried hopes of demystifying the scheme, promoting health literacy, and encouraging a culture of preventive healthcare among the youth. The triumph earns Afia Kobi Ampem Girls Senior High School a ticket to the national grand finale of the NHIA Inter-School Quiz Competition, where it will represent the Middle Belt. The girls’ school will face the winners of the Northern Belt and Southern Belt in the grand finale scheduled for 30 November 2026, to determine the overall national champion. Speaking on behalf of her teammates, Jacqueline Aygabeng of Afia Kobi Ampem Senior High School expressed excitement over the team’s victory, describing it as a well-deserved reward for their hard work and consistent preparation. “As we did today, we believe that for the preparations that we have already put in place and the ones that we are going to do in our schools, it is going to prepare us enough and with the power and prayers of God, we are going to excel in whatever competition that is ahead of us,” Jacqueline said. Jacqueline noted that beyond the trophy, the competition had equipped the students with valuable knowledge about the National Health Insurance Scheme that will benefit them long after the contest. According to her, the learning experience has been mutually beneficial for both the students and society, as the students are now better placed to serve as ambassadors of the scheme in their communities. The initiative, which involves 48 senior high schools nationwide, is being implemented with the Ministry of Education and the Ghana Education Service (GES) under the School Health Education Programme.

items.title: Adjei-Mensah Korsah questions government’s housing delivery, cites gaps in Saglemi and rent-to-own targets
items.description: Former Minister for Local Government and Rural Reorganisation, Martin Adjei-Mensah Korsah, has questioned the government’s progress on housing commitments, arguing that the 2027 Budget fails to adequately account for earlier targets and outstanding projects. In an assessment of the 2027 Budget’s provisions for the Works, Housing and Water Resources sector, shared on Facebook on Wednesday, November 25, the former Minister said several housing commitments remained unreconciled, raising concerns about delivery timelines, funding and access to affordable homes. He cited the Saglemi Housing Project, noting that the 2026 Budget had set a target of making 8,000 units habitable in 2026, while the 2027 Budget schedules 1,506 units for delivery in 2027, including 700 by March. He said the government had not explained the change in scope or accounted for the earlier target. Mr Adjei-Mensah Korsah also pointed to the 800 housing units at Kpone, which remain reported at 80 per cent completion, despite an earlier ministerial statement in April indicating that the project was expected to be completed by September 2026. He said revised timelines should not replace an account of previous commitments. On rental and homeownership programmes, he said the previous year’s commitment to provide 10,000 additional rent-to-own beneficiaries had not been properly reconciled with the latest figures. The 2027 Budget reports 917 rental-assistance beneficiaries as of September 2026 and 5,647 beneficiaries since the programme began, but these are different schemes and measures. The former Minister further raised concerns about inconsistencies in the financing of the Housing Fund. He said paragraph 1557 of the Budget provides GH¢500 million, while Appendix 4A lists GH¢1 billion, with the latter matching a pledge made by the President in October. He also questioned the new provision of approximately GH¢103 million for district housing, against the GH¢500 million earmarked for the programme in 2026, and called for a clear account of the funds and progress made. Mr Adjei-Mensah Korsah argued that the government must move beyond announcing housing numbers and demonstrate how its programmes will make homes affordable. He called for the publication of prices, deposits, financing terms and monthly payment limits, alongside delivery targets for different income groups. He said the government should also publish a funded completion and handover plan prioritising viable housing projects nearing completion, while ensuring that informal-sector workers are assessed through verifiable income, cash flow and savings arrangements.

items.title: Stanbic-Asantehene Invitational Golf Tournament strengthens relationships and excellence through sport
items.description: The 2026 Stanbic-Asantehene Invitational Golf Tournament brought together golfers, business leaders and distinguished guests at the Kumasi Royal Golf Club for two days of sporting excellence, networking and relationship-building. Held under the patronage of Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the tournament reaffirmed sport’s power to foster connections, promote excellence, and create opportunities for engagement among stakeholders from diverse sectors. Addressing the leadership of Stanbic and golfers, the Asantehene underscored golf’s importance as a discipline that promotes integrity, patience, focus, and respect, values equally important in leadership, business, and community development. He commended the continued partnership between traditional institutions and the private sector in advancing initiatives that unite people and contribute to national development. The Asantehene also noted that platforms such as the Stanbic-Asantehene Invitational Golf Tournament provide a unique opportunity for individuals and organisations to build lasting relationships while supporting the growth of sport in Ghana. Speaking at the event, Stanbic Bank Ghana’s Chief Executive, Kwamina Asomaning, said the tournament reflects the Bank’s commitment to fostering meaningful connections among its clients, partners and stakeholders. “At Stanbic, we believe strong relationships are fundamental to progress. This tournament provides an excellent platform for bringing together business leaders, professionals and golf enthusiasts in an atmosphere that encourages collaboration, shared learning and lasting partnerships,” he said. Mr. Asomaning added that the Bank remains committed to supporting initiatives that create value beyond banking by promoting platforms that contribute to personal development, business growth and community engagement. For her part, Chidinma Braye-Yankee, Head of Brand and Marketing at Stanbic Bank Ghana, highlighted sport’s role as a powerful connector across industries and communities. “Golf provides a unique opportunity for people from different backgrounds and industries to connect, build relationships and share experiences. Through the Stanbic-Asantehene Invitational, we are proud to support an initiative that brings together the values of excellence, integrity and community,” she said. She explained that the Bank’s partnership with the Asantehene reflects its appreciation of institutions and traditional leadership that continue to play an important role in community development and national progress. According to Mrs. Braye-Yankee, the tournament forms part of Stanbic Bank’s broader strategy of creating meaningful experiences that deepen relationships with clients and stakeholders while supporting the growth of sporting excellence in Ghana. The two-day competition featured golfers from across the country and provided opportunities for friendly competition, networking and camaraderie, further cementing the tournament’s reputation as one of Ghana’s premier golfing events. Through the Stanbic-Asantehene Invitational Golf Tournament, Stanbic Bank Ghana and the Asantehene continue to demonstrate the value of partnership in promoting sport, strengthening relationships and advancing a culture of excellence. Caption: Otumfuo Osei Tutu II (Center) with Kwamina Asomaning, Chief Executive, Stanbic Bank and Executives of the Bank.

items.title: Newmont credits 99% Ghanaian workforce for Ahafo success, pledges deeper local leadership
items.description: Newmont Corporation has credited its predominantly Ghanaian workforce, which accounts for approximately 99 per cent of its more than 11,000 employees, with powering two decades of operational success at its Ahafo South mine, while pledging deeper technical and leadership roles for local professionals and businesses in the years ahead. Speaking at a grand durbar in Kenyasi in the Asutifi North District over the weekend to mark 20 years of commercial production at Ahafo South, Newmont President and Chief Executive Officer Natascha Viljoen placed Ghanaian workers, contractors, and emerging talent at the centre of the company’s milestone celebration. “The effect of Newmont’s investments over more than 20 years cannot simply be measured in ounces of gold. These investments have created an enduring foundation for jobs, economic activity and national development,” Ms. Viljoen told traditional leaders, government officials, employees, and community members. Since commercial production began at Ahafo South in 2006, the operation has grown to encompass both surface and underground mining, rising to become Ghana’s largest gold mine and one of the top three in Africa, with over 10 million ounces of gold produced. Ms. Viljoen noted that the 11,000-strong workforce figure represents thousands of careers built, families sustained, and technical competencies sharpened. Crucially, the skills developed at Ahafo have positioned Ghanaian professionals to serve not only within domestic operations, including the neighbouring Ahafo North mine, which achieved commercial production a year ago, but also across Newmont’s global portfolio and the wider international mining industry. She added that over the past two decades, operational safety, technology adoption, and progressively stronger mining capabilities have all been anchored on the safety, development, and career progression of Ghanaian colleagues. Across the Ahafo South and Ahafo North operations, approximately 80 percent of operational work is executed through contractors, creating sustained business opportunities for Ghanaian companies and service providers based in host communities. In 2025 alone, Newmont channelled roughly US$905 million through procurement and supply-chain activities, directly supporting local entrepreneurs, suppliers, and secondary employment nationwide. Looking ahead to the next 20 years and a long-term strategy to extend the life of the Ahafo beyond 2050, Ms. Viljoen emphasized that human capital development remains central to Newmont’s future in Ghana. Through the Newmont Ahafo Development Foundation (NADeF), which has received over US$77 million in company contributions, Newmont is supporting the University of Mines and Technology (UMaT) branch campus in the region. Following a visit to the campus ahead of the durbar, Ms. Viljoen described it as a practical investment in grooming the next generation of Ghanaian mining professionals to sustain the sector well beyond the lifespan of current mines. With approximately US400 million in capital expenditure approved for 2027 and up to US4 billion in potential future district investments under evaluation, Ms. Viljoen projected even deeper technical and leadership roles for young Ghanaians, alongside stronger participation by domestic firms in the mining value chain. She also credited the dedication and operational excellence of Newmont’s Ghanaian workforce for Newmont Ghana Gold Limited being ranked Ghana’s number one company at the Ghana Club 100 Awards for three consecutive editions. “A future in which Ghanaian companies, through partnership, technology and skills, take on ever larger roles in the mining economy, with the capability to lead, that is the commitment Newmont wants to carry forward in Ghana,” Ms. Viljoen indicated.

items.title: Sissala East MP Bataglia vows to fix Tumu Municipal Hospital
items.description: It was not a rally. It was not a campaign stop. It was Sissala East asking, plainly, for what it needs to survive – and the people in power answering in their presence with no place to hide. From chiefs in smocks to a young nursing student holding a microphone with shaking hands, one by one they stood up. No long grammar. No big English. Just truth. Tumu did not come to clap. Tumu came to talk. Centre for the youth First, the Chief of Jaana, Kuoro Bennin Yussif Douri, opened the floor: “Give us a community centre. Our youth have nowhere to meet.” Sissala East Municipal Chief Executive, Adamu Yakubu, answered, “It’s on course. It’s in our plan. Look at Chalo — abandoned before, now under construction. Tumu’s own will come.” Hospital with no snake venom Then the Chief of Kong and Headmaster of Kanton Senior High School, Kuoro Mahamudu Zakaria Savei, came with pain: a hospital with no snake venom. The Upper West Regional Minister, Charles Lwanga Puozung, gave a date, not just talk: “Before the end of this month, vaccines must reach Tumu.” He added, “NHIA is free. Dialysis twice a week is free. Mahama Care has already saved 15 people in Upper West — some surgeries costing over GH₵500,000. The Municipal Hospital will be well equipped next year” And he warned, “Check your Hepatitis B. You look strong, then in 48 hours we bury you. It is killing us.” MP Bataglia: “I have been part of the work” But it was the Member of Parliament (MP) for Sissala East, Mohammed Issa Bataglia, who took the Municipal Hospital matter head-on — and gave the hall details, not just promises. He admitted the problem is real. “The issue of the Municipal Hospital, if you are confronted with it like my brother Fatawu, your best indicator — that’s very true,” he said. He said a lot of efforts have been made to get the hospital functioning, and he has been an integral part of that work, including through his private work as Country Director for a foundation. The X-ray story that shook the hall Mr Bataglia recalled a sad event last year, when the Minister for Education, Haruna Iddrisu, and the Deputy Minister for Communication, Technology and Innovation, Mahama Adam Sukparu, were coming to attend a graduation programme at the school and had an accident. One of the biggest challenges they faced was the lack of an X-ray machine at the hospital. He said a benefactor has since promised an X-ray machine, and just last week in Parliament, he made him speak to the person who will buy it for Tumu. Bigger than equipment: Light But Mr Bataglia said the bigger challenge is not just equipment — it is retrofitting the hospital itself. “The lighting system has a problem,” he said. “I have on my own brought about nine ultrasound machines. About eight of them are down just because they don’t have stable lights. We are working towards that.” Doctor Raymond, monitors and 50 beds He praised the current doctor at the hospital, Dr Raymond Danso Sei, saying he is doing very well, and has already started using Internally Generated Funds (IGF) to do some renovations around the facility. “I have agreed with him. He talked about patient monitors. I am going to have three of those procured,” Mr Bataglia said. He added that by the end of the year, not less than 50 beds will arrive to be distributed to the hospital and other facilities. On the mortuary, he said he and the MCE have taken it very seriously and are pushing for it to be done very soon. “We are doing everything possible to make sure that we get things done right,” he said. On the nursing school and jobs Turning to Modesta Latu Hasukulo, Students’ Representative Council (SRC) President of the Nursing College, Mr Bataglia said she was right — and reminded the hall that the school itself started from the National Democratic Congress (NDC) administration. “The fact that you even have a school to attend, the applause will first go to us before we take the infrastructure,” he said. “But we are doing everything possible to make your study good there.” He also addressed unemployment, describing it as a major challenge facing the constituency and the country at large. “The challenge of unemployment is quite a problem, and the numbers today are not the numbers of yesterday,” he said. He appealed to students to also play a role: “Don’t just attend and leave. Attend and make it better. So together we work to get the place better.”

items.title: Senegal reinstated as 2025 African champions, Morocco to contest decision
items.description: Senegal were reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners on Tuesday after the sport’s highest court upheld their appeal against being stripped of the title, ruling that the referee’s decision to resume the match fell under the “field of play” doctrine. The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) panel set aside the Confederation of African ‌Football (CAF) Appeal Board’s decision that had forfeited Senegal’s 1-0 extra-time win and awarded Morocco a 3-0 result. The Misinformation Monitor newsletter rounds up international misinformation narratives, with a “Real or Fake?” quiz in every edition. Sign up here. CAF said in a statement it “respects the CAS award and will take all the necessary measures to implement it”. The panel found that “the referee (Jean-Jacques Ndala of the Democratic Republic of Congo) did not commit any error of law”, CAS Secretary General Matthieu Reeb said. CAS confirmed the result of the January 18 final in Rabat as 1-0 to Senegal. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) said the decision was a triumph ​for “sporting fairness” and that the “outcome of a match is determined solely on the field of play, under the protection of sports law”. FSF President Abdoulaye Fall said the federation was ​ready to put the matter behind it and offered an olive branch to its Moroccan counterparts. “The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice ⁠for sport,” Fall said in a statement. “I wish to strongly reaffirm the bonds of brotherhood that unite us with the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) and the Moroccan people. “Senegalese football now looks ​firmly towards the future with confidence and enthusiasm in an Africa united around the values of sport.” MOROCCO TO CONTEST DECISION The FRMF said in a statement that it will contest the decision, alleging there ​had been contact between its Senegalese counterpart and CAS arbitrator Ulrich Haas in the days leading up to the verdict. However, an FSF spokesperson told Reuters: “That is false. There was no telephone contact on Sunday or on any other day.” CAS added: “Ulrich Haas strongly denies any direct contact at any moment with the parties involved in this procedure”. Senegal walked off the pitch for 14 minutes in the final after a penalty awarded against them late in regulation time. The players returned before ​the match resumed, Morocco missed the spot kick and Pape Gueye scored the winner in extra time. CAS said the referee’s decision to resume play fell within his sole authority, and that ​the effects of that decision were limited to the pitch. Morocco’s federation had argued that the referee’s decision fell outside the field of play doctrine and that the walk-off breached Articles 82 and 84 of the Cup ‌of Nations ⁠regulations. Those articles apply only when a referee calls off a match permanently, the panel said, so did not apply here. The panel acknowledged the referee made his decision under extreme tension but said that did not justify calling it “arbitrary.” The panel also said that CAF had already sanctioned the FSF, Senegal’s then-coach Pape Thiaw and players Iliman Ndiaye and Ismaila Sarr in separate disciplinary proceedings. LEGAL PROCEEDINGS The FRMF said it will “initiate all necessary legal proceedings to challenge the CAS decision” after it complained about alleged contact made between FSF President Fall and CAS arbitrator Haas 48 hours before the ruling was issued. It can do so by appealing to the Swiss ​Federal Supreme Court, which is the only court ​with jurisdiction to hear the challenge. French sports ⁠law expert Gerald Simon chaired the CAS panel, with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Haas, a Hamburg-based attorney and professor of law at the University of Zurich. The ruling was unanimous. “There could only be one winner in this final, just as there could only be one winner in this ​legal process,” CAS’s Reeb told reporters. “The law has spoken. I think we simply have to accept the decision of the Court of Arbitration ​for Sport. “The team’s (Senegal’s) temporary withdrawal ⁠from the field was not followed by the abandonment of the match. If the referee had blown the final whistle, he could have done so, and perhaps things would have turned out differently. The CAS arbitrators considered that the referee was within his rights,” he added. Senegal striker Sadio Mane said he hoped the matter did not drive a wedge between the two nations. “I send a message of respect ⁠and encouragement to ​the Moroccan people and the players of Morocco,” Mane said in a statement. “They’ve done a great course and can ​be proud of it. I wish them all the best for the future. Senegal and Morocco are two brotherly peoples. May the passion of football continue to bring us closer.” CAS said it had issued the full grounds to the parties on ​Tuesday and that the award will be published in due course unless confidentiality is requested.

items.title: UNHCR Bangladesh: Quarterly Protection & Solutions Report - Q3 2026 | July - September
items.description: Countries: Bangladesh, Myanmar Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. 1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY PROTECTION ENVIRONMENT SNAPSHOT The protection environment across the 33 camps and on Bhasan Char further deteriorated in Q3, driven by worsening insecurity and economic hardship. The Protection Sector’s Q3 Joint Protection Monitoring Report, which combines monitoring inputs from seven partners including UNHCR, recorded a 39% increase in serious security incidents from Q2, led by abductions and kidnapping for ransom, alongside rising armed group tensions, recruitment activity and violent assaults. Tighter border controls raised the share of refoulement incidents from 14% in 2025 to 31% in 2026 and, for the first time, affected refugee card holders. Maritime departures more than doubled compared with 2025. Gender-based violence and child protection risks, including child marriage and sexual violence against children, also increased. Cross-border movements declined during the Q3 rainy season. The number of people affected by refoulement incidents fell by 74% from Q2 before rising steadily in September as travel conditions improved, while community sources reported increased new arrivals due to deteriorating security in Myanmar. The 15 September suspension of new-arrival registration (the Government-approved biometric identification process for enrolling newly arrived Rohingya to access humanitarian assistance, except shelter allocations) heightened vulnerability for new arrival families, who now have no access to food or assistance. UNHCR is in discussions with authorities to address concerns about eligibility and recommend improvements to the joint Government of Bangladesh–UNHCR registration process with increased involvement of government personnel. No timeline has yet been confirmed to resume enrolment. The Protection Sector avoided pipeline breaks in Q3, but reduced funding for the 2026 Joint Response Plan (JRP) forced service reductions. Data reported by the Sector showed a 30–40% reduction in community-based protection activities as of 30 September, affecting some 150,000–200,000 refugees. Overall, only 21% of people with specific protection needs (30,322) received targeted support. With chronic underfunding of prevention and risk mitigation activities, an estimated 150,000 children and adolescents remained at risk of abuse, exploitation, violence and neglect, and more than 500,000 women and girls at risk of gender-based violence. Against this backdrop of reduced services, harmful coping mechanisms increased in the Cox's Bazar camps as economic hardship deepened. Three trends reflect the worsening environment: Domestic trafficking and exploitative labour grew, with economic hardship contributing to 75% of trafficking cases, up from 61% in Q2. Abductions and kidnappings rose from 78 incidents in Q2 to 84 in Q3 (according to UNHCR data). Intimate partner violence also remained highly prevalent—linked to unemployment, drug use, online gambling, polygamy, family conflict, harmful gender norms and dowry disputes. Meanwhile, UNHCR led transformation efforts to save costs and improve efficiency—including shifting awarenessraising to digital and refugee-led approaches; replacing static information and feedback centres with mobile teams; joint planning and stronger referral pathways; and integration of protection programming and resources through 280 multipurpose centres.

Binationaux, immigrés : qui aurait le plus à craindre d’une victoire de Marine Le Pen ?
items.description: Référendum sur l'immigration , préférence nationale, interdiction du port du voile dans l’espace public, remise en cause du droit du sol… Les promesses électorales de Marine Le Pen , favorite des sondages pour la présidentielle de 2027, font légitimement peur. Qui doit le plus redouter l'accession au pouvoir de la fille de Jean-Marie Le Pen : les Français d’origine étrangère (les binationaux ), les immigrés en situation régulière ou les sans-papiers ? TSA a interrogé Fayçal Kaddour, adjoint au maire de Vitry-sur-Seine et fondateur de l'association de la diaspora algérienne « Djazpora ». Fayçal Kaddour : la « préférence nationale » va impacter les immigrés réguliers Pour l'élu d’origine algérienne, ce sont clairement les étrangers, même en situation régulière, qui vont d’abord subir les premières conséquences d’une victoire de l'extrême-droite qui a annoncé qu'elle mettra en place la « préférence nationale » pour l'accès à certains emplois, au logement social, aux prestations sociales… De plus, souligne Fayçal Kaddour, le Rassemblement national (RN) veut remettre en cause le droit du sol. « Donc les enfants qui naîtront en France de parents étrangers ne seront plus français si facilement. C’est une remise en cause profonde », dit-il. Autre conséquence, obtenir la nationalité pour un étranger en situation régulière « va devenir un véritable parcours du combattant », anticipe M. Kaddour. Sans-papiers : moins de régularisations et plus d'expulsions Les binationaux, sur ce sujet de la nationalité, ne seront pas concernés. Cependant les étrangers en situation régulière vont être impactés. Les étrangers en situation irrégulière seront, eux, directement touchés par la politique de gestion des flux migratoire que promet de mettre en place le tandem Marine Le Pen – Jordan Bardella s’il arrive à l’Elysée en 2027. Les régularisations seront très difficiles et les expulsions vont repartir à la hausse, prévient l'adjoint au maire de Vitry-sur-Seine. Marine Le Pen change de discours concernant les binationaux Outre les immigrés, légaux ou non, le Rassemblement national a ciblé aussi par le passé les binationaux notamment ceux originaires du Maghreb. Lors de la campagne des législatives de 2024, Jordan Bardella avait proposé d'interdire aux détenteurs de la double nationalité l’accès à certaines fonctions « sensibles ». La proposition avait suscité un tollé. À quelques mois de la présidentielle de 2027, Marine Le Pen tente de ratisser large et multiplie les mea culpa concernant ses précédentes prises de position. La semaine passée, elle a admis avoir commis une erreur en proposant, lors des présidentielles de 2012 et 2017, d’interdire la double nationalité. Dans les faits, les binationaux issus du Maghreb notamment d’Algérie auront du mal à accéder aux hautes responsabilités en France. Sur l’Islam, elle soutient désormais que son problème est avec « la charia » et « l’islamisme » et non pas avec la religion musulmane. En revanche, le reste des mesures controversées du parti extrémiste, comme l’interdiction du port du foulard islamique, tient toujours… L’article Binationaux, immigrés : qui aurait le plus à craindre d'une victoire de Marine Le Pen ? est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Le Soudan, microcosme de ce qui succède à l’ordre mondial libéral
items.description: Testez le Grand Continent . Les idées et les analyses qu’on ne trouve nulle part. Mais que vous verrez bientôt partout. Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois Parce qu’il a été à maintes reprises le théâtre d’interventions multilatérales visant à prévenir les atrocités et à stabiliser la situation humanitaire, le Soudan a souvent servi de baromètre de l’état de santé de l’ordre mondial libéral 4 . Plus de deux millions de personnes auraient trouvé la mort durant la deuxième guerre civile soudanaise Second Sudanese Civil War (1983-2005) », Strategic Studies Institute (SSI) , février 2025.'> 5 , entre 1983 et 2005. Au Darfour, durant la première décennie des années 2000, quelque 300 000 personnes ont perdu la vie selon les estimations d’observateurs internationaux, et 2 à 3 millions ont été déplacées. Genèse de la « responsabilité de protéger » À l’époque, trouver une solution aux conflits soudanais était une priorité pour les États-Unis et les pays européens. La deuxième guerre civile soudanaise n’a pris fin qu’en 2005, à l’issue d’une intense médiation menée à la fois par la troïka composée des États-Unis, du Royaume-Uni et de la Norvège, et par les voisins africains du Soudan réunis au sein de l’IGAD. Immédiatement après l’accord de 2005, la Norvège s’est par exemple engagée à consacrer environ 252 millions de dollars au cours des trois années suivantes afin d’aider le pays à se remettre de plusieurs décennies de guerre Norway contributes 252 million dollars to Sudan », ReliefWeb , 11 avril 2005.'> 6 . L’ampleur des préoccupations occidentales et des ressources diplomatiques alors mobilisées pour intervenir dans les conflits semble aujourd’hui, soit vingt ans plus tard, presque inimaginable. Dans les années 2000, le Soudan a accueilli deux vastes missions de maintien de la paix des Nations unies Past peacekeeping operations .'> 7 . La première, l’Opération hybride Union africaine-Nations unies au Darfour (MINUAD), a duré plus de 13 ans ; elle s’est achevée en 2020. La seconde, la Mission des Nations unies au Soudan (MINUS), a duré plus de six ans et s’est conclue en 2011. Elles poursuivaient deux objectifs principaux. Il s’agissait d’une part de prévenir le génocide au Darfour, et d’autre part de garantir la mise en œuvre de l’accord de paix qui mettrait fin à la guerre civile entre le gouvernement de Khartoum et le Mouvement populaire de libération du Soudan (SPLM) avec son Armée populaire de libération du Soudan (SPLA). Cette dernière mission, qui comptait environ 10 000 soldats et de nombreux personnels civils, s’est achevée après le référendum sur l’indépendance du Soudan du Sud de janvier 2011. En juillet de la même année, le Soudan du Sud était accueilli au sein de la communauté internationale comme le plus jeune État du monde. Dans ce contexte – marqué par les efforts internationaux visant à mettre fin aux guerres civiles au Soudan et aux déplacements massifs de population qui en ont résulté –, le diplomate sud-soudanais Francis Mading Deng développe le concept de « souveraineté en tant que responsabilité ». Deng s’est activement confronté à ces questions en tant que Représentant du Secrétaire général des Nations unies pour les personnes déplacées à l’intérieur de leur propre pays de 1992 à 2004. De nombreux experts voient dans ce concept la genèse du principe international de responsabilité de protéger (R2P) Recovering African contestation and innovation in global politics : Francis Deng and sovereignty-as-responsibility », International Theory , Vol 16, n°3, 18 novembre 2024, pp. 354-381.'> 8 La responsabilité de protéger .'> 9 dont l’adoption par l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies, dans le Document final du Sommet mondial de 2005, a marqué un point culminant pour la légitimité de l’ordre mondial libéral. Telle que formulée par Deng et d’autres, la R2P visait à trouver un équilibre entre la souveraineté – entendue comme le droit à la non-ingérence pour tout État – et le devoir de la communauté internationale de veiller à ce que chaque État protège le bien-être de ses propres citoyens. Le Soudan : victime du post-américanisme ? Aujourd’hui, le conflit au Soudan peut être décrit comme une guerre mondiale en miniature. Les chiffres sont si colossaux qu’ils rendent difficile la compréhension de l’ampleur de la tragédie qui s’y déroule. Selon l’Agence des Nations unies pour les réfugiés, plus de 14 millions de personnes ont dû fuir leur foyer depuis le début de la guerre en avril 2023 Agence des Nations unies , « Sudan : 14 million displaced ; hunger and attacks on health continue as war enters fourth year », 10 avril 2026.'> 10 , et quelque 8,6 millions sont aujourd’hui déplacées à l’intérieur du pays. Par ailleurs, on dénombre au moins 4,4 millions de réfugiés soudanais ayant fui le pays – et ce, notamment vers des pays voisins comme le Tchad, l’Égypte et le Soudan du Sud, qui ont bien du mal à faire face à cet afflux. Plus de trois ans et demi plus tard, des combats intenses se poursuivent dans la région centrale du Kordofan, au Darfour, ainsi que dans l’État du Nil Bleu, au sud-est du Soudan. Souvent éclipsé par d’autres guerres malgré l’horreur des violences qui y sont commises, le conflit a néanmoins fait l’objet d’une analyse particulièrement commentée : celle de la journaliste et historienne américaine Anne Applebaum, publiée dans The Atlantic en septembre 2025 à l’issue de reportages derrière les lignes tant des Forces armées soudanaises (SAF) que de leurs adversaires – les Forces de soutien rapide (RSF). Selon elle, « aucune statistique ne peut exprimer le sentiment d’absurdité, de vide de sens, que la guerre a laissé derrière elle » This Is What the End of the Liberal World Order Looks Like », The Atlantic , 6 août 2025.'> 11 . Face à la destruction physique de villes comme Khartoum, Anne Applebaum a qualifié ce conflit de « plus nihiliste de la planète », écrivant avec une pointe de désespoir que « l’ordre mondial libéral a déjà pris fin au Soudan, et il n’y a rien pour le remplacer ». En effet, si des pays comme le Royaume-Uni ont fait du Soudan une priorité humanitaire depuis 2023 UK aid to Sudan , 15 octobre 2025.'> 12 , leurs budgets réduits sont aujourd’hui à peine suffisants pour combler le vide laissé par la baisse de l’aide étrangère américaine. De son côté, l’Union européenne coordonne des efforts multilatéraux pour faire face aux crises humanitaires et aux déplacements forcés EU and Member States pledge over €812 million in response to crisis in Sudan », 15 avril 2026.'> 13 ; ceux-ci n’ont toutefois pas permis de modifier de manière significative la trajectoire du conflit. À bien des égards, ce qui se passe au Soudan illustre l’abandon par la communauté internationale – et en particulier par l’Occident – des principes établis de longue date de l’ordre mondial libéral. En quelques années, le Soudan est devenu le jouet d’un large éventail d’acteurs s’étendant du Moyen-Orient à l’Afrique, en passant par la Russie et jusqu’à la Colombie. À la suite des coupes budgétaires opérées par l’administration Trump aux dépens d’organismes tels que l’Agence des États-Unis pour le développement international (USAID), même l’engagement à prévenir la propagation de la famine s’est trouvé affaibli What Comes After the Refugee Camp », Noema , 23 juin 2026.'> 14 . Aujourd’hui, le Soudan serait-il ainsi victime d’un monde anarchique et post-américain, comme le déplore Applebaum dans son article ? Dans sa conclusion, l’historienne décrit du moins un monde qui n’a pas encore pleinement pris forme, dans lequel « le colonialisme appartient depuis longtemps au passé », où la guerre froide est certes terminée, mais où l’ordre international s’est irrémédiablement effondré. Un retour à l’ère précoloniale Ce qui se passe au Soudan et ailleurs n’est toutefois pas l’émergence de l’anarchie, mais un retour aux schémas précoloniaux. De nombreux observateurs ont commis l’erreur de conclure à l’anarchie en raison de ce que l’historien Richard Reid appelle le « raccourcissement de l’histoire africaine ». Il désigne par là « le détachement du présent tumultueux de l’Afrique – et de son passé récent – des schémas plus profonds de changement et de continuité ». Aucun pays n’a sans doute autant souffert que le Congo – autrefois connu sous le nom de Zaïre – de la réification du passé colonial par les spécialistes en sciences sociales et les élites modernisatrices. À la fin du XIXe siècle, le journaliste et explorateur britannique Henry Morton Stanley s’est vu attribuer le surnom de Bula Matari, ou « briseur de rochers », pour « son exploit consistant à mener une caravane de porteurs transportant des bateaux à vapeur démontés sur le terrain accidenté entre l’estuaire du fleuve Zaïre et les vastes cours d’eau navigables s’étendant vers l’intérieur des terres depuis Kinshasa ». Comme le souligne Zala Lusibu N’Kanza (plus connue sous le nom de Sophie Kanza), première femme à avoir occupé le poste de ministre en République démocratique du Congo, « pour tous les Bakongo, le nom de Bula Matari était synonyme de terreur ». Le monde précolonial aurait ainsi été anéanti dans le sillage d’un État colonial et postcolonial en pleine ascension et en pleine modernisation. De l’autre côté de l’Atlantique, pour la génération fondatrice des politologues africanistes américains, comme Crawford Young, les institutions politiques, économiques et sociales de la période précoloniale avaient été réduites à néant, car elles n’avaient pas la résilience nécessaire pour offrir une alternative à l’État modernisateur. Qu’en est-il aujourd’hui ? Malgré l’ampleur de la tragédie humaine qui se déroule dans tout le Nord-Est de l’Afrique – englobant non seulement le Soudan, mais aussi le Soudan du Sud, l’Éthiopie, l’Érythrée, la Somalie et le Somaliland –, le monde post-américain décrit par Applebaum n’est pas uniquement synonyme de chaos. Des tendances claires se dessinent, même au milieu de cette violence née de la fracture de l’État. L’une des plus évidentes est le développement de schémas politiques et commerciaux ressemblant à ceux de l’ère précoloniale. La longue domination de l’État colonial n’était pas le résultat d’un démantèlement des sociétés africaines, comme l’ont longtemps supposé les politologues américains. Il en va de même pour ce chaos durable qui entache la période postcoloniale : celui-ci ne se réduit pas à des rivalités ethniques. Au contraire, la persistance de l’ordre colonial dans des pays comme le Soudan est le fruit de l’héritage de ses infrastructures. La durabilité singulière des infrastructures construites pendant la domination européenne du bassin du Nil résulte d’un concours de circonstances historiques. Dans son nouvel ouvrage , The Alibi of Capital : How We Broke the Earth to Steal the Future on the Promise of a Better Tomorrow (Verso, 2026), le théoricien politique Timothy Mitchell soutient qu’au tournant du XXe siècle, une nouvelle capacité à « escompter » l’avenir a été inventée. Mitchell considère cette capacité comme une technologie politique « découlant du fait que le temps peut être contrôlé – par la construction d’un appareil politique capable de s’emparer de l’avenir et de le coloniser de manière fiable ». Si la formule peut paraître très abstraite, Mitchell précise : « L’ampleur et l’étendue des voies de transport et des réseaux énergétiques, ainsi que le développement urbain, les projets d’irrigation et d’autres programmes de grande envergure, dépendaient non seulement de la durabilité matérielle, mais aussi de la pérennité des dispositifs juridiques, de l’autorité, de la contrainte et de la justification. » Si le Soudan est bien souvent perçu comme une marge négligée de l’Empire colonial, ce pays a été le théâtre de l’un des plus grands investissements de l’Empire britannique dans l’agriculture industrielle. Le gigantesque projet agricole irrigué de Gezira, l’un des rares monuments du colonialisme visibles depuis l’espace, avait été initialement prévu dans les années 1920 pour irriguer à terme un million d’acres. Les responsables britanniques parlaient ouvertement du potentiel du projet de Gezira à devenir un second delta du Nil artificiel, une gigantesque plantation de coton pour l’Empire. Des années 1920 jusqu’aux années 1970, où le projet a rencontré des difficultés financières, les chemins de fer, les barrages, les ports, les infrastructures financières et économiques du pays étaient mis au service de ce projet, de même que la main-d’œuvre soudanaise. Dans les années 1990, cette situation a changé avec l’essor du secteur pétrolier. Toutefois, les oléoducs et les raffineries avaient alors toujours tendance à être implantés selon les modèles établis à l’époque coloniale The New Kings of Crude : China, India, and the Global Struggle for Oil in Sudan and South Sudan , Oxford University Press, 15 octobre 2014.'> 15 . Ces modèles ont perduré, notamment parce que les canaux d’irrigation et les voies ferrées étaient littéralement inscrits dans le sol, dans la terre et l’acier. Une autre raison explique aussi la persistance de ces modèles : le Soudan s’est intégré aux marchés financiers mondiaux grâce à des prêts destinés à des investissements garantis par l’accès aux marchés d’exportation. À l’origine, il s’agissait du coton, puis du pétrole brut, et aujourd’hui, de l’or. L’ordre international libéral fragile Lorsque le politologue John Ikenberry a écrit sur l’ordre international libéral, il a fait remarquer qu’« il existe une hypothèse optimiste sous-jacente à l’internationalisme libéral selon laquelle les États peuvent surmonter les contraintes et coopérer pour résoudre les dilemmes de sécurité, mener une action collective et créer un système ouvert et stable » Liberal Internationalism 3.0 : America and the Dilemmas of Liberal World Order », Perspectives on Politics , vol. 7, n° 1, mars 2009, pp. 71-87.'> 16 . Pourtant, Ikenberry admet également que la nature collective de ce système a toujours été davantage une aspiration qu’une réalité. Il reconnaît que, depuis 1945, les États-Unis ont joué le rôle de propriétaire et d’exploitant de ce système, se voyant accorder des privilèges et des responsabilités particuliers. C’est ainsi que l’on peut comprendre ce chaos décrit par Applebaum, qui s’est installé au Soudan depuis que les États-Unis ne sont plus disposés à porter ce fardeau historique. Mais quelle nouvelle lecture apparaîtrait si on appréhendait ce chaos comme n’étant que la dissolution des ordres politiques ayant permis de pérenniser les investissements des États coloniaux et postcoloniaux ? Il suffit pour cela de regarder ce qu’il en est du coton et du pétrole brut, ces dernières années. Bien qu’il s’agisse de matières premières différentes, l’État central pouvait contrôler en grande partie leur exportation, soit en gérant directement la production, soit en délivrant des licences de production et de vente à des clients privilégiés. L’essor des exportations d’or du Soudan depuis 2013 est remarquable par l’incapacité totale de l’État à contrôler ce commerce. Pour le Soudan, la tragédie est amplifiée par la hausse de près de 200 % des cours de l’or au cours de cette période 10 Year Gold Price Chart in USD .'> 17 . L’État soudanais a donc été privé de cette manne du fait de sa propre impuissance, puis de la guerre. Aujourd’hui, une partie du défi pour les autorités soudanaises réside donc dans le fait que la production artisanale d’or, contrairement au contrôle des champs pétrolifères et des oléoducs ou à l’irrigation du coton, ne présente pas les goulets d’étranglement infrastructurels centraux que l’État colonial et postcolonial avait su si bien exploiter à des fins fiscales Black Gold, Liquid Metal : The Political Economy of Gold in Sudan », Noria Research , 21 juillet 2025.'> 18 . L’autre dilemme pour l’État soudanais tient à l’effondrement, à l’échelle régionale, du tabou interdisant de traiter avec certains acteurs infra-nationaux. En conséquence, l’or provenant des mines du Darfour aboutit souvent dans les souks de Dubaï, sans jamais passer par le gouvernement central. De même, des soldats soudanais chargés de surveiller la frontière entre l’Arabie saoudite et le Yémen peuvent être recrutés et déployés sans jamais passer par les Forces armées soudanaises (SAF). Les RSF, une entité à mi-chemin entre une force paramilitaire et une société commerciale, effectuent bon nombre de ces transactions et administrent de vastes portions du Soudan pour le compte de leurs investisseurs. Le retour des schémas précoloniaux sous des apparences contemporaines Ce qui ressemble à du chaos révèle en réalité des schémas précoloniaux. Au cours des trois ans et demi qui se sont écoulés depuis le début des combats entre les Forces armées soudanaises (SAF) et les RSF, de nouvelles routes commerciales et d’approvisionnement militaire sont devenues de plus en plus visibles. Dans les premières décennies qui ont suivi l’indépendance du Soudan en 1956, l’essentiel de l’activité économique s’écoulait des provinces vers Khartoum, puis le long des voies ferrées jusqu’à Port-Soudan, sur la mer Rouge. Le gouvernement tirait l’essentiel de ses recettes de la taxation des importations et des exportations qui empruntaient cette route bien fréquentée. Au cours des deux premières années de combats, les RSF contrôlaient Khartoum et ont tout mis en œuvre pour briser l’ancienne route commerciale coloniale. Pendant cette période, le gouvernement soudanais s’est replié à Port-Soudan, tandis que les RSF ont établi une capitale rivale à Nyala, au Darfour-Sud. La guerre a, sans que personne l’ait voulu, remis au jour d’anciens schémas de formation de l’État datant du XIXe siècle. Quels étaient les mécanismes à l’œuvre ? Suakin et les autres ports soudanais de la mer Rouge affirmaient leur allégeance à un lointain gouvernement ottoman, et résistaient à leur intégration au royaume de Sennar – sans parler du Darfour. Les élites de Suakin cherchaient souvent à être rattachées à la province ottomane du Hedjaz ou à Aden, dans la péninsule arabique. En 2023, ce schéma a failli se répéter, lorsque le gouvernement soudanais a été contraint de se replier temporairement à Port-Soudan après la chute de Khartoum. Mais un fait peut-être plus marquant encore est la réapparition d’anciennes routes commerciales vers le nord, l’ouest et le sud du Darfour, à la faveur de la guerre. Les Forces armées soudanaises (SAF), qui tiennent Port-Soudan, comme les RSF ont commencé à se tourner vers les anciennes routes commerciales traversant le désert. La plus célèbre était le Darb el-Arba’īn, ou « route des Quarante Jours », l’une des grandes routes de la traite, menant du nord du Darfour à Assiout, dans le sud de l’Égypte. D’autres routes commerciales menaient vers le nord, en Libye, où les RSF seraient soupçonnées d’avoir établi des bases sous la protection de Khalifa Haftar, l’homme fort de l’Est libyen qui contrôle aujourd’hui la partie orientale du pays How we found an RSF military camp in the Libyan desert », Centre for Information Resilience , 31 juillet 2025.'> 19 . De même, les routes commerciales reliant le sud du Darfour au Soudan du Sud ont été réactivées pour réapprovisionner les RSF. Ces routes aboutissent souvent en Ouganda, au Kenya et en République centrafricaine. Toutes échappent au contrôle du pouvoir central. La nouvelle importance prise par ces anciennes routes commerciales a culminé avec la proclamation, le 15 avril 2025, d’un gouvernement rival par la TASIS TASIS announces formation of Government of Peace and Unity », 15 avril 2025.'> 20 , ou Alliance fondatrice du Soudan, soit précisément deux ans après le déclenchement de la guerre. Réunis en février 2025 à Nairobi, la capitale du Kenya, pour y signer leur charte fondatrice, les dirigeants de la TASIS avaient tenté de consolider une alliance entre les RSF, certaines factions du Mouvement populaire de libération du Soudan-Nord (SPLM-N) – à la fois groupe armé et parti politique – et certains dirigeants Baggara Baggara », 101 Last Tribes .'> 21 . Les Baggara comptent plus de six millions de personnes, se réclamant d’une ascendance arabe, réparties du sud du Kordofan jusqu’au lac Tchad. Fondée en 2013, l’organisation des RSF – avec en son centre la famille arabe de son chef Muhammad Hamdan Daglo Musa (dit « Hemedti »), originaire du Darfour – fait elle-même écho à un épisode de la fin du XIXe siècle. Celui-ci débute par la création d’un empire commercial privé par al-Zubayr Rahma al-Mansur, plus connu sous le nom de Zubayr Pacha Zubair Pasha Remembered », Middle East Monitor , 28 juillet 2020.'> 22 . À l’origine simple assistant commercial sans grand relief auprès d’un négociant égyptien, Zubayr avait fondé dès les années 1860 l’une des plus grandes sociétés commerciales. Celle-ci opérait dans ce que nous appelons aujourd’hui le Soudan du Sud. Ses activités ont été décrites en ces termes dans un article rétrospectif du « Middle East Monitor » : « [Il envoya] des hommes “à travers les terres des Dinka, des Jur et des Bongo ; la compagnie atteignit les Golo, qui vivaient alors entre les fleuves Kuru et Kpongo”. Ils achetaient des plumes d’autruche et de l’ivoire pour les commercialiser à Khartoum, au Caire et au-delà. » Ibid. '> 23 Dans les années 1870, il était passé du statut de commerçant prospère à celui de souverain d’un territoire souvent appelé Deim Zubayr. Il contrôlait une vaste région englobant le Bahr al-Ghazal (dans l’actuel Soudan du Sud) et le Darfour, avec une armée d’environ 12 000 soldats, dont beaucoup étaient des esclaves. Selon l’historienne Tsega Etefa Tsega Etefa , professeur à la Colgate University.'> 24 , dans un article publié dans le Journal of Oromo Studies : « À la fin des années 1860, al-Zubayr était “le plus éminent et le plus prospère des princes marchands opérant dans le Bahr al-Ghazal”. Il faisait le commerce d’esclaves et d’ivoire ; cependant, les mouvements antiesclavagistes menés par des explorateurs égyptiens et européens dans la vallée du Nil commencèrent à faire pression sur lui. C’est pourquoi “il s’arrangea avec les tribus Baggara du sud du Darfour pour que ses caravanes d’esclaves traversent leur territoire en direction du nord, en contournant le Nil”. Vers la fin des années 1860, “il atteignit le statut de souverain pratiquement indépendant”. La force expéditionnaire du gouvernement égyptien “fut complètement vaincue par lui, et les autorités égyptiennes, prenant conscience de la personnalité dominante à laquelle elles avaient affaire, le nommèrent gouverneur du district.” » Au départ, la base de Zubayr se situe dans les zones frontalières du sud, entre le Darfour et le Bahr al-Ghazal. Le Darfour, en tant qu’entité politique indépendante, n’est conquis qu’en 1874, lorsque les forces de Zubayr réussissent ce que les armées ottomanes et égyptiennes de Muhammad Ali n’avaient pas pu accomplir en 1821 : la conquête du sultanat des Fur, jusqu’à sa capitale, El Fasher. Les parallèles avec les RSF semblent s’imposer d’eux-mêmes, et sont devenus particulièrement frappants fin octobre 2025, lorsque les RSF se sont emparées d’El Fasher après dix-huit mois de siège, au prix de massacres de civils largement documentés. Les RSF ont ainsi pris le dernier bastion majeur de l’armée au Darfour et ont consolidé leur capacité à s’approvisionner vers le nord via la Libye et vers le sud, à travers le Soudan du Sud jusqu’en Afrique de l’Est. L’émergence du Kordofan en tant que région contestée constitue un autre écho du XIXe siècle. Les armées de Muhammad Ali, maître de facto de l’Égypte de 1805 à 1848, avaient partiellement pacifié la région dans les décennies qui ont suivi l’invasion égyptienne de 1821. Elles n’étaient toutefois pas parvenues à maintenir un contrôle stable. À bien des égards, cela ressemble à la situation actuelle au Kordofan, où des villes comme El-Obeid – qui compte environ un demi-million d’habitants, sans compter les déplacés – restent la cible d’attaques fréquentes Pas de refuge sûr : déplacement et survie à El Obeid », U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants , 3 septembre 2026.'> 25 , alors que des forces rivales se disputent la domination de la région. Mais c’est peut-être dans l’autonomie relative du SPLM-N – parti politique et groupe armé dont les bastions se situent dans le sud du Kordofan – que les échos du XIXe siècle apparaissent le plus clairement. Depuis la sécession du Soudan du Sud en 2011, le SPLM-N a joué tour à tour un rôle de médiateur et de perturbateur entre Khartoum et Djouba. Au XIXe siècle déjà, les plaines avaient été facilement conquises, mais les montagnes de Nuba s’étaient avérées très difficiles à contrôler durablement. Une faction, le SPLM-N Al-Hilu, qui contrôle principalement les zones autour des montagnes de Nuba dans le Kordofan du Sud, s’est rangée du côté des RSF ; tandis qu’une autre faction, le SPLM-N Agar, qui contrôle certaines parties de l’État du Nil Bleu, s’est rangée du côté des Forces armées soudanaises (SAF). Ce faisant, les deux groupes ont préservé l’autonomie des régions frontalières entre les RSF, les SAF et le Soudan du Sud. Une organisation frontalière – qui semble plus soucieuse de la préservation de sa propre autonomie que de l’issue de la guerre – s’est ainsi retrouvée à opérer des deux côtés du conflit. Les stratégies qu’elle a ainsi mises en œuvre présentent d’autres parallèles surprenants avec le passé. On peut ainsi établir un parallèle avec le royaume de Taqali, situé au nord-est des montagnes de Nuba au Soudan Speaking, Writing, and Authority : Explorations in and from the Kingdom of Taqali », Comparative Studies in Society and History , vol. 30, n° 2, avril 1988, pp. 200-224.'> 26 . Celui-ci a prospéré entre environ 1780 et 1884, et son autonomie relative s’est prolongée jusqu’en 1969, soit bien après l’indépendance du Soudan. Nos recherches menées au sein de la collection « Soudan » de l’université de Bergen, en Norvège, montrent qu’au XIXe siècle, les dirigeants de Taqali avaient recouru à une stratégie similaire. Celle-ci consistait à rechercher la protection et la reconnaissance tant de l’État du Darfour que de celui de Sennar – alors en déclin. Cela passait par une double vassalité, envers l’un et l’autre, tout en s’efforçant de préserver leur autonomie. L’effondrement de l’État soudanais auquel nous assistons aujourd’hui n’est pas non plus le fruit du hasard. Au contraire, parallèlement au recul de l’ordre mondial libéral, on voit réapparaître des ordres politiques qui s’étaient manifestés pour la dernière fois avec une telle clarté au XIXe siècle. Ces schémas se répètent car ils reposent sur des liens commerciaux, politiques et économiques qui ne dépendent pas des infrastructures mises en place pendant la période coloniale. La pérennité de ces dernières s’est en effet érodée, à mesure que les institutions de l’ordre mondial libéral qui les soutenaient se sont effondrées. À la place des schémas commerciaux, des infrastructures et de l’ordre politique qui semblaient autrefois faire inévitablement partie du monde postcolonial, nous assistons à la réapparition d’anciennes voies d’échanges. Par exemple, on observe la résurgence des routes transsahariennes, des routes commerciales vers l’Afrique de l’Est et centrale, ainsi que des liaisons est-ouest traversant le Sahel et la mer Rouge. En Afrique du Sud, des voix s’élèvent pour réclamer de défaire l’unité forgée en 1910 par l’Union sud-africaine. Celle-ci avait réuni quatre colonies britanniques : le Cap, le Natal, le Transvaal et la colonie de la rivière Orange – ces deux dernières étant les anciennes républiques boers du Transvaal et de l’État libre d’Orange, annexées par la Grande-Bretagne à l’issue de la guerre de 1899-1902. Depuis plus d’une décennie, le Yémen connaît quant à lui un processus de redécoupage qui rappelle celui du XIXe siècle. Plus au nord, l’agression russe a elle aussi remis en cause la stabilité des frontières – ici, celles de l’Europe de l’Est. Ce ne sont là que quelques exemples illustrant à quel point la stabilité qui a caractérisé la seconde moitié du XXe siècle ne peut être considérée comme acquise. Alors que nous réfléchissons aux modèles susceptibles de mieux expliquer les recompositions du pouvoir après l’ordre libéral, il apparaît de plus en plus pertinent de se tourner vers la carte du XIXe siècle comme exemple de concurrence politique et de frontières mouvantes. L’article Le Soudan, microcosme de ce qui succède à l'ordre mondial libéral est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence
items.description: Click to expand Image Women take part in a demonstration against the military coup in Mandalay, Myanmar, on July 10, 2021. © 2021 STR/AFP via Getty Images Every year during the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence women’s rights defenders come together to remember women facing violence—including those we have lost—and to renew the struggle for gender equality. This year we face growing gender inequality, as the rights of women and girls are rolled back and threatened by authoritarianism and conflict in many countries. Across all regions, governments and powerful anti-rights movements seek to dismantle hard-won rights for women and girls. Technology is adding new dimensions to abuse, from online harassment and surveillance to digitally enabled threats, violence, and sexualized deepfake images; women politicians are often targeted. In the United States and Russia, authorities are dismantling reproductive rights. In Africa, lawmakers, with support from foreign conservative groups, are promoting a charter aiming to roll back women’s rights across the continent. In Argentina, funding for preventing GBV has been scrapped. As armed conflict increases across the globe, more women and girls are living in proximity to fighting. During conflict, women and girls face heightened risks of sexual and gender-based violence, displacement, and economic insecurity, often with little access to protection or justice. In Sudan and Democratic Republic of Congo, sexual violence is a common feature of ongoing conflict with survivors facing significant barriers to obtaining protection, services, and justice. In Myanmar, women political prisoners are tortured. Reproductive rights are a casualty of Israel’s closures in the West Bank, its ongoing blockade of the Gaza Strip, and its continued attacks on Palestinian health facilities. But activists refuse to accept erosion of women’s rights. In March, the Commission on the Status of Women called for strengthening access to justice for all women and girls. In April, the European Parliament passed a resolution calling for consent to be the determining factor in rape legislation across the EU. In November, Hungary announced it would ratify the Istanbul Convention, strengthening women’s rights protections. Activists from Afghanistan are fighting to have gender apartheid recognized as an international crime. Activists are also pushing back against technology-facilitated abuse, demanding that companies protect, rather than endanger, women and girls. In different countries young women are leading protest movements to challenge corruption and authoritarianism. Rights defenders will not lose hope.

items.title: No missing funds in $2.04bn Duke Oil crude cargoes — NNPC
items.description: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) has dismissed reports alleging that $2.04 billion realised from crude oil cargoes lifted by Duke Oil Company Incorporated, now NNPC Trading S.A., was unaccounted for, insisting that all transactions were fully reconciled. The company said the $2.04 billion represented the gross value of 29 cargoes whose proceeds were set off against the cost of refined petroleum products supplied to Nigeria under the Direct Sale Direct Purchase (DSDP) programme. In a statement by its Chief Corporate Communications Officer, Andy Odeh, NNPC said the absence of separate dollar receipts for some cargoes did not indicate missing funds. “No separate receipt appears because the crude sale proceeds were set off against the product purchase price, as the contracts provide,” it stated. Under the DSDP programme, participating traders lifted crude oil in exchange for refined petroleum products, including petrol, for the Nigerian market. NNPC explained that while crude was priced in dollars, products supplied were sold in naira, with transactions reconciled and captured in the audited financial statements of the relevant entities. The company said all 59 cargoes referenced in the reports were accounted for, adding that 30 were paid for in dollars, while proceeds from 28 cargoes, valued at approximately $1.96 billion, were remitted in naira to the NNPC Group Treasury or NNPC Upstream Investment Management Services accounts. The remaining cargo, a February 2023 Bonga tax-oil lifting valued at about $75.9 million, was paid into the then designated Federal Inland Revenue Service dollar account. On Duke Oil’s ownership, NNPC said it was incorporated in 1989 as its wholly owned trading subsidiary, adding that the relationship was documented in its corporate history, audited financial statements and NEITI’s 2023 industry report. It maintained that transactions between the company and its subsidiaries were disclosed as related-party transactions under International Financial Reporting Standards. NNPC reaffirmed its commitment to transparency and accountability, but warned that it reserved the right to take legal action against publications it considered false or misleading. The post No missing funds in $2.04bn Duke Oil crude cargoes — NNPC appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Madagascar backs Morocco’s autonomy plan for Western Sahara
items.description: Madagascar has reaffirmed its support for Morocco’s territorial integrity and its proposed autonomy plan for Western Sahara, strengthening diplomatic ties between the two African nations. The two countries announced their position on Monday in a joint communiqué issued at the end of the second session of the Morocco-Madagascar Joint Cooperation Commission in Rabat. Morocco’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccan Expatriates, Nasser Bourita, and Madagascar’s Foreign Affairs Minister, Alice N’Diaye, co-chaired the meeting. Madagascar reaffirmed its commitment to the principle of territorial integrity of United Nations member states and expressed support for Morocco’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. The country also endorsed Morocco’s autonomy initiative and welcomed United Nations Security Council Resolution 2797, which recognises genuine autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as potentially one of the most viable solutions to the Western Sahara dispute. Madagascar’s renewed backing comes amid Morocco’s diplomatic efforts, led by King Mohammed VI, to secure broader international support for its autonomy proposal. Western Sahara remains disputed, with Morocco proposing autonomy under its sovereignty while the Polisario Front continues to push for independence. Madagascar’s Foreign Affairs Minister was on a working visit to Rabat to advance bilateral cooperation between the two countries.
