items.title: South-East 400-km $100m gas pipeline, recipe for region’s industrial growth — SEDC
items.description: By Chinedu Adonu For decades, businesses and industries across Nigeria’s South-East region have depended on generators for their daily operations at a high cost. From the manufacturing clusters in Aba, Abia State, to the industrial workshops in Nnewi, Anambra State, the commercial centres of Onitsha, the business communities of Enugu and the productive enterprises of Imo and Ebonyi states, they all face the high cost and unreliability of electricity, forcing them to spend millions of naira to power their generators just to ensure that they remain in business. It has not been easy for a region whose economic strength is deeply rooted in entrepreneurship, manufacturing, commerce, and small-scale industries. Indeed, the energy challenge remains a major obstacle to industrial expansion as they spend huge resources powering their factories. All of them, including small businesses, struggle with rising operational costs. Will the proposed 400-kilometer South-East Gas Distribution Pipeline Project, with an initial investment budget of approximately $100 million, be a game changer for them? This initiative by the South-East Development Commission, SEDC, is planned to connect natural gas resources around the region to industrial and commercial centres across the five states in the region. It was unveiled at the South- East Gas Infrastructure Investment and Project Development Ceremony in Enugu on October 27, 2026. The initiative is a partnership between SEDC and GasSync Limited, NNPC Gas Marketing Limited and other stakeholders. President Bola Tinubu, represented at the ceremony by the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Rt., Hon. Benjamin Kalu, described the project as an important step towards addressing the infrastructure deficit which has constrained the productive capacity of the South-East region. “There is a sound familiar to every manufacturer in Aba, Nnewi, Onitsha, Enugu and across the South-East. It is the sound of a generator,” Tinubu noted, adding that the resilience of South-East entrepreneurs should no longer be an excuse for inadequate infrastructure. “Our manufacturers should not have to spend more on generating electricity than on expanding production. Our young entrepreneurs should not find that the greatest obstacle to their ambition is the cost of keeping their machines running,” he pointed out. According to the President, Nigeria’s natural gas resources should be measured not merely by what lies beneath the soil but by the factories they power, the jobs they create and the prosperity they bring. A 400-km economic corridor At the heart of the initiative is a proposed regional gas distribution network designed to connect the Assa North-Ohaji gas processing project in Imo State to major industrial and commercial centres across the South-East. Presenting the project details, GasSync representative, Callistus Mba explained that the pipeline would begin from the gas source around Assa North-Ohaji, extending to Owerri, Aba, Onitsha, Enugu and eventually, Ebonyi State. The proposed network, he explained, will cover approximately 400 kilometers, with construction expected to commence simultaneously from two major points to accelerate delivery. According to Mba, the construction strategy followed consultations with the Enugu State Government, which expressed concern that beginning from Imo and extending sequentially to the other states could prolong delivery. “We are going to start at Assa North and at Onitsha at the same time. We will construct from Onitsha to Enugu and Ebonyi while simultaneously working from Assa North to Owerri and Anambra,” he explained. The arrangement, he explained, is intended to fast-track construction and ensure that the northern sections of the network are developed alongside the southern corridors. The proposed infrastructure will comprise different pipeline sizes to accommodate the varying pressure requirements and distribution needs of the regional market. He explained that a 24-inch high-pressure pipeline would transport gas from the source to Owerri, while 18-inch pipelines would serve the regional distribution corridors. Smaller 12-inch pipelines would connect major industrial customers. The network, he further explained, will also incorporate city-gate facilities, pressure reduction and metering stations to ensure that gas is delivered at appropriate pressure levels and under safe operating conditions. Demand for gas already exists One of the major considerations behind the project is the growing demand for affordable and reliable energy among manufacturers and commercial establishments across the region. Mba disclosed that GasSync had identified more than 150 prospective customers across the five states, while surveys indicated potential demand of approximately 254 million standard cubic feet of gas per day. He noted that some businesses already depend on expensive virtual gas transportation arrangements, including compressed natural gas and liquefied natural gas delivered by road from other parts of the country. The proposed pipeline, he said, would provide a more direct and potentially cost-effective transportation option. “What GasSync is intended to do is ensure that there is a pipeline coming through so that these virtual pipelines, which are expensive and require delays in delivery, will be taken off,” Mba stated, saying that the company has identified prospective industrial customers in different states and is already engaging some of them on supply arrangements. According to him, in Abia, discussions are ongoing with Geometric Power, while other industrial customers have been identified in Imo and Anambra. In Enugu, the state government’s interest in reviving former industrial establishments, including ANAMMCO and the Niger Gas Company, presents additional opportunities for gas utilisation. Mba also disclosed that the company was making provisions to accommodate gas resources that could be developed within Enugu State, including the possibility of utilising coal-bed methane. In Ebonyi, the focus includes agro-processing and other gas-dependent enterprises. The company, he disclosed, has also identified additional potential gas supply connections around the region, including the Kwale Gas Processing Plant, activities around Obeaku/OB3 and other existing gas infrastructure. The initial phase requires approximately $100m Tinubu, in the course of his speech, noted that government could not finance every development ambition from the public treasury, stressing the need to deploy public resources strategically to attract larger pools of private capital. “This is the model I expect from our development institutions: identify strategic economic opportunities, prepare credible projects, commit public resources responsibly and mobilise private capital at a scale government budgets alone cannot achieve,” he stated. For the SEDC, the project is also consistent with the broader South-East Vision 2050 framework, which seeks to promote coordinated regional development and economic integration. A new future for South-East youths For Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah, the gas project represents an important opportunity to reposition the region as a competitive industrial and investment destination. He commended Tinubu for establishing the SEDC, describing it as a long-awaited institutional framework for the industrialisation of the South-East. Mbah said the investment agreement signed at the ceremony represented the commencement of the investment process and demonstrated the importance of bringing the private sector into regional infrastructure development. “What we have just signed here today is an investment agreement, meaning that investment has commenced,” the governor said. He described the financial arrangement as an innovative model that could bring together government institutions, private investors and other development partners to finance critical infrastructure. According to him, the project aligns with the long-standing aspiration of the South-East governors to establish a common economic market and industrialise the region collectively. He said the project would create opportunities for young people to build their futures within the region rather than migrate elsewhere in search of employment. “Before now, it was our young people running out of the region in search of greener pastures. But with what we have now, our young people can sit back and find their future here in the region,” he said. Mbah further disclosed that research had indicated the existence of significant unidentified gas deposits in Enugu State, expressing optimism that the proposed infrastructure would provide opportunities for their future utilisation. Governors rally behind the project The other South East states also expressed support for the initiative, with their representatives highlighting the potential benefits to manufacturing, employment and regional economic development. Imo State Deputy Governor, Lady Chinyere Ihuoma Ekomaru, described the project as timely, particularly with the growing interest of companies in accessing gas from the Assa North-Ohaji facility. Anambra State Deputy Governor, Dr Onyekachukwu Ibezim, urged host communities along the pipeline corridors to support the project, stressing the importance of community participation in its successful implementation. He said that Anambra state is also planning for future population growth and the infrastructure requirements that would accompany increased economic activities. “We will clap for you when we begin to feel the impact of what you are doing,” Ibezim told the commission, emphasizing that the project’s success would ultimately be measured by its tangible benefits. Ebonyi State Deputy Governor, Mrs. Patricia Obila, described energy as fundamental to industrial development, noting that inadequate power supply had contributed to the decline of several enterprises in the region. She expressed hope that the proposed gas infrastructure would help revive moribund industries and create employment opportunities. Obila assured the project promoters of Ebonyi State’s support, particularly in facilitating the development of the pipeline within the state. Also speaking, the Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Regional Development, Dr. Mary Ogbe, described the SEDC as an important institution for improving the living standards of people in the region. She assured the governors that the commission was established to complement their development efforts rather than compete with state governments. She also encouraged investors to take advantage of the emerging opportunities. The road to first gas: 2027-2028 While the project has attracted considerable political and commercial support, its actual delivery will depend on the successful completion of several critical stages. The Gas company has assured that procurement processes have commenced and funding arrangements are advancing towards financial close, while engineering, procurement, and construction preparations are progressing. Construction is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027, with the target of achieving readiness for start-up and first gas in the second quarter of 2028. However, the project promoters acknowledge that several issues must be addressed to keep the schedule on course. These include securing the necessary regulatory approvals, obtaining licenses, completing right-of-way arrangements, engaging host communities and finalizing agreements with prospective gas customers. Beyond the pipeline: The bigger economic question The significance of the proposed gas distribution network extends beyond the transportation of natural gas. For the South-East, its potential value lies in whether it can stimulate a new wave of industrial investments, reduce production costs, revive struggling manufacturing establishments, and create sustainable employment. According to President Tinubu, the ultimate measure of the project should not be the agreements signed at the ceremony but the economic activities generated by the infrastructure. “We are not investing in pipelines for their own sake. We are investing in the industries, businesses and jobs those pipelines will make possible,” he said. As Tinubu observed, the future the region seeks should no longer be defined by the sound of generators struggling to keep businesses alive, but by the sound of factories operating at full capacity. For the South East, that is the promise of the proposed gas infrastructure project. The challenge now is turning that promise into reality. items.title: Ethiopia: Anticipatory action to mitigate drought impacts on vulnerable pastoral communities - October 2025
items.description: Country: Ethiopia Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations Please refer to the attached file. Scaling up anticipatory action is a strategic investment: saving lives and livelihoods today while reducing humanitarian needs over time. Introduction The pastoral lowlands of Ethiopia have endured compounded climate shocks since the 2020–2022 drought, the worst in four decades. The drought resulted in an urgent need for life-saving and life-sustaining assistance for 17.2 million people in Ethiopia, in addition to causing widespread displacement and the loss of an estimated 6.8 million animals. Favourable rainfall across much of the country in 2024 improved agricultural production. However, in February 2025, early warning analyses and forecasts by the Ethiopian Meteorological Institute (EMI) and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development’s Climate Prediction and Applications Centre indicated a high probability of drought conditions during the March–April–May (MAM) season in parts of southern and southeastern Ethiopia. The MAM season is crucial for replenishing pasture and water resources and supporting crop production and community livelihoods. Below-average rainfall and the anticipated drought were expected to exacerbate the already fragile food security, nutrition and livelihood conditions of communities in parts of Oromia and Somali regions. In line with the national anticipatory action (AA) protocol, the Ethiopia Disaster Risk Management Commission and the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) advised partners in the country to activate AA interventions in priority areas to mitigate the impact of the anticipated drought. In response, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) implemented activities in 32 districts (woredas) – 15 in Oromia region and 17 in Somali region – identified as highly vulnerable and at risk of severe impacts.

items.title: Political Violence: Dying for nothing as a Nigerian politician?
items.description: By Jide Ajani From the First Republic to the Fourth, politicians have been murdered, opposition figures silenced and political supporters killed. Yet, beyond the initial outrage, Nigeria has perfected the art of forgetting its dead. What, then, is the value of dying for a political cause in a country that cannot even preserve the memory of its political martyrs? The alleged assassination attempt on the former Deputy Senate President, Ovie Omo-Agege, two days ago, in Uduere community of Ughelli North LGA of Delta State, brings this odd reality into focus once again. Worse, many innocent, ordinary Nigerians have lost their lives while supporting or opposing politicians, only becoming part of an unidentified statistical figure. There is something inescapably tragic about dying while politicking in Nigeria. You could spend a lifetime building a political movement, challenging an unjust system, defending an electoral mandate, or fighting for an idea about your country’s future – or just being loud for nothing like a former, two-time state governor from the South West, or a former Rep and Senator from the North Central. You could become a household name, command enormous political influence and acquire a place in the nation’s history. Then, one morning, gunmen arrive, bullets are fired, and your life is terminated. There will be outrage. Condemnations will pour in. Politicians will issue statements, newspapers will publish editorials (like this), civil society organisations will demand justice, and the police will announce investigations. And then, Nigeria happens, and the people move on. The murder will become another entry in the country’s expanding archive of unresolved political crimes. The victim’s name will gradually disappear from public conversations, except when anniversary commemorations provide an opportunity for political speeches. Even the circumstances of the death may eventually become blurred by competing narratives, political expediency and the convenient amnesia of a nation. Is it, therefore, worth dying for Nigeria’s politics? The question intends to interrogate a society that celebrates political martyrs without demonstrating a corresponding commitment to preserving their legacies or establishing the truth about their deaths. On Monday, November 23, 2026, four persons were killed during an alleged assassination attempt on the former Deputy Senate President, Ovie Omo-Agege, two days ago, in Uduere Community of Ughelli North LGA of Delta State. Over a dozen were said to have been injured. Mind you, in an outburst of emotive frustration about happenings inthe political sphere, the self-same Omo-Agege had used the phrase ‘ ig and die’. He was to later clarify that he was merely drawing attention to the need for credible elections. A bloody inheritance Political violence has accompanied Nigeria’s political evolution almost from independence. The January 15, 1966 military coup was a defining bloodbath. Among the prominent political victims were Prime Minister Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, Northern Premier Sir Ahmadu Bello, Western Premier Chief Samuel Ladoke Akintola and Federal Finance Minister Chief Festus Okotie-Eboh. They were not anonymous casualties. They occupied the commanding heights of the First Republic and represented competing political interests and constituencies. Their assassination, alongside the killing of senior military officers, fundamentally altered Nigeria’s political trajectory. The July 1966 counter-coup brought another round of killings, including Head of State Major-General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi and Western Region Governor Colonel Adekunle Fajuyi. Although these were killings arising from military coups and counter-coups rather than conventional electoral assassinations, they established a dangerous precedent: political disagreements and struggles for power could be settled through the elimination of human beings. On February 13, 1976, another military coup attempt claimed the life of Head of State General Murtala Mohammed. He was assassinated in Lagos by officers involved in the unsuccessful coup led by Lieutenant-Colonel Buka Suka Dimka. The military era also saw attacks on prominent government opponents. In October 1995, Chief Alfred Rewane, businessman, political financier and prominent supporter of the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO), was murdered in his Ikeja residence. The killing occurred during General Sani Abacha’s military dictatorship. The circumstances generated widespread suspicions of political motivation, but no satisfactory public resolution followed. The following year, on June 4, 1996, Kudirat Abiola was assassinated by unknown gunmen while travelling along the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway. She had become a prominent campaigner for the validation of her husband Moshood Abiola’s June 12, 1993 presidential mandate. Her murder was widely perceived as an attempt to silence the pro-democracy movement. Subsequent proceedings produced a conviction of Major Hamza al-Mustapha and another accused person, but the Court of Appeal overturned the convictions. The circumstances and ultimate accountability for her killing have remained contested. There were other disturbing incidents. Alex Ibru, publisher of The Guardian and a former minister, survived an assassination attempt in February 1996 after being shot in Lagos. Gani Fawehinmi, the human rights lawyer, was also the subject of a reported attack on the prison facility where he was detained, although he was not there at the time. The Fourth Republic: democracy and its dead The return to civilian government in 1999 raised expectations that constitutional politics would make political violence less attractive. Those expectations were soon tested. On December 19, 2001, Osun State legislator Odunayo Olagbaju was stabbed to death in Ile-Ife. Four days later, on December 23, Chief Bola Ige, the serving Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, was shot dead in his Bodija residence in Ibadan. Ige was a formidable politician, former governor of Oyo State, intellectual and prominent member of the Alliance for Democracy. His murder, against the background of the political crisis involving the governor and deputy governor of Osun State, sent shockwaves through the country. Several suspects were arrested and prosecuted, but the accused were discharged and acquitted in June 2004. The actual perpetrators have not been established through a successful prosecution. What happened to the national outrage that followed the murder of a sitting Attorney-General? On March 5, 2003, Harry Marshall, a senior opposition politician and national vice-chairman of the All Nigeria Peoples Party (ANPP), was murdered in his Abuja residence. Armed men reportedly forced their way into his home at about 3 a.m., tied up his security guard, and shot him in his bedroom. His killing occurred days before the commencement of the party’s presidential campaign. The police initially investigated extensively, but the motive was never conclusively established. Some suspected political connections; the authorities also considered armed robbery. In February 2004, Chief Aminasoari Dikibo, a prominent PDP national vice-chairman, was murdered while travelling in Delta State. His death generated allegations of political conspiracy, but no definitive public resolution emerged. Then came July 27, 2006. Engineer Funsho Williams, a prominent Lagos politician and governorship aspirant, was found murdered in his Ikoyi residence. His hands were reportedly tied, and the post-mortem evidence presented during the subsequent proceedings indicated death by strangulation. Several people were prosecuted. In 2014, however, a Lagos High Court discharged and acquitted the defendants after finding that the prosecution had failed to establish a sufficient connection between them and the murder. Another aspirant, Dr Ayo Daramola, was murdered at his home in Ekiti State in August 2006. The catalogue does not end there. Ogbonnaya Uche was killed in Owerri in 2003; Barnabas and Abigail Igwe, a lawyer and his wife, were murdered in Onitsha in September 2002; and Dipo Dina, an Ogun State governorship candidate in the 2007 election, was shot dead in January 2010. These are unfinished investigations, abandoned questions and families left without satisfactory answers. Other election-related attacks have included the killing of candidates, party officials and campaign workers. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have documented the wider pattern of electoral violence, including attacks that never attracted the national attention accorded to the deaths of prominent politicians. The national habit of forgetting What is perhaps more disturbing than the killings is the country’s relationship with the memory of those killed. Nigeria has become remarkably efficient at converting tragedy into political folklore and then consigning the folklore to oblivion. The murder of Bola Ige should have become an enduring national lesson about the vulnerability of public institutions. Instead, the country largely returned to its political routines. Funsho Williams should have remained a reference point in conversations about the safety of political aspirants. Harry Marshall should have become a symbol of the dangers confronting opposition politics. Alfred Rewane and Kudirat Abiola should occupy permanent places in the country’s democratic memory. Yet, their names are invoked intermittently, often by politicians seeking temporary moral authority. The philosopher George Santayana famously warned: “Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” The warning is particularly relevant to Nigeria. Forgetting is not necessarily an innocent failure of memory. When a society fails to demand answers, preserve records and sustain public attention, it creates the conditions in which impunity can flourish. Cicero’s observation that “the life of the dead is placed in the memory of the living” offers another uncomfortable reflection. What kind of afterlife does a nation confer on those whose sacrifices it cannot remember? Others have learned to remember Nigeria is not the only country with unresolved political assassinations. Sweden has never conclusively established who murdered Prime Minister Olof Palme, who was shot dead on a Stockholm street on February 28, 1986. Although investigators identified a likely suspect in 2020, he was dead and could not be prosecuted. Swedish prosecutors subsequently maintained that there was insufficient evidence to reopen the investigation. Pakistan continues to wrestle with the circumstances surrounding the December 27, 2007 assassination of former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto. A United Nations Commission of Inquiry examined the circumstances of her death but did not identify the individuals ultimately responsible for the assassination. Lebanon’s former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri was killed in a massive bomb explosion in Beirut on February 14, 2005, alongside other victims. The subsequent United Nations-backed investigation and Special Tribunal produced important findings and convictions, although questions about the full chain of responsibility and political accountability have persisted. The difference is not that these countries have solved every political murder. It is that their investigations, public inquiries, official records and continuing debates demonstrate that the death of a political leader need not become a forgotten footnote. There are also examples of murdered leaders whose deaths did not extinguish their causes. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee, on April 4, 1968. He was 39 years old. He had spent his life fighting racial discrimination through non-violent resistance and civil rights activism. His death was a devastating blow, but it did not terminate the movement. His words, philosophy and political struggle became enduring reference points in American public life. His legacy was institutionalised through memorials, national commemorations and continuing civil rights advocacy. The United States did not simply mourn King and move on. It preserved his memory as part of its national identity. King’s legacy illustrates something important: a political assassination can destroy a human life, but it need not destroy the cause that gave the life meaning. And what of MKO Abiola? Perhaps the most troubling example of Nigeria’s complicated relationship with political memory is Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola. He died in detention on July 7, 1998, while the struggle to reclaim his mandate from the annulled June 12, 1993 presidential election remained unresolved. Abiola’s death did not end the controversy surrounding his mandate. Indeed, more than two decades after his death, the political interpretation of June 12, his democratic credentials and his place in history continue to be contested and appropriated by different political interests. The declaration of June 12 as Democracy Day was an important official recognition. But recognition must mean more than appropriating a dead man’s political capital. His historical significance should be examined honestly, including the political compromises, convictions and sacrifices that defined his life. There is something deeply ironic about a country that celebrates a man for the mandate he fought to reclaim but cannot protect the historical integrity of his struggle from partisan manipulation. Is it worth dying for? This brings us back to the original question: Is it worth allowing yourself to be killed for Nigerian politics? There is no universal answer. People have a right to stand for their convictions, defend democracy and challenge injustice. A society without courageous people willing to confront abuse of power would be a society without meaningful political progress. But courage must not be confused with recklessness, and martyrdom must not become an excuse for national irresponsibility. Albert Camus, in The Myth of Sisyphus, wrote: “The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart.” Perhaps the meaning of political life lies not in the eventual reward of public recognition but in the principles one defends and the institutions one helps to build. Yet, a nation also has obligations to its dead. It must investigate their murders, prosecute offenders where evidence permits, preserve historical records and resist the temptation to turn their sacrifices into disposable political slogans. A politician’s life should not be measured exclusively by the office he occupied, the money he accumulated or the number of followers who attended his funeral. It should also be measured by the ideas he advanced, the institutions he strengthened and the generations he inspired. The tragedy of Nigeria is not simply that Bola Ige, Harry Marshall, Funsho Williams, Kudirat Abiola, Alfred Rewane and so many others died violently. It is that we have not demonstrated sufficient determination to establish the truth about their deaths and protect the historical meaning of their lives. A country that forgets its murdered leaders diminishes the value of public service and discourages the next generation from believing that political conviction is worth defending. Perhaps the most painful question is not whether these men and women died for nothing; it is whether Nigeria, by its persistent refusal to remember, investigate and learn, has ensured that they did. items.title: HIV infections could rise from historic lows starting next year, UN says
items.description: The head of the UN agency for AIDS warned on Tuesday ‌that new HIV infections could begin rising from historic lows next year due to funding cuts and anti-rights campaigns , just as the world is on the verge of eradicating the disease. “We are on the cusp of ​ending AIDS – this has been the greatest story of global health – and just when ​we should finish it, cuts and the rolling back of human rights ⁠is threatening to take away our gains,” Winnie Byanyima, executive director of UNAIDS, told Reuters. “We ​haven’t got the data yet, but we see the signs. We see all the signs ​of reversals,” she added, predicting that 2027 data would start reflecting rising infections. The latest UNAIDS data released on Tuesday shows new infections last year at an all-time low of 1.2 million, down from a peak of 3.5 million people in 1994, despite last year’s drop of nearly a fifth in international funding. Byanyima, from Uganda, said the impact of the funding cuts could start to show up soon in ‌numbers ⁠of infections as some countries struggle to fill the gap on their own, resulting in prevention clinic closures and staff reductions. “All these are signs of what is to come, which is likely to be rising new infections,” she said, adding that numbers were already increasing in ​parts of South America. As ​well as funding cuts, ⁠Byanyima said that a global political backlash against women’s access to sexual and reproductive health and LGBTQ rights posed a “serious threat”. The UN aims ​to end HIV/AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. Rising pressure ​on the ⁠UN to restructure has led to deep cuts at its 30-year-old AIDS agency. It has already dismissed half its staff and stopped work in about 30 countries, but its board rejected a ⁠plan to dissolve ​it altogether last month. “It will (now) be a more gradual ​shift to a smaller size. The core work will remain,” said Byanyima, who leaves her post in December to ​focus on activism on issues such as global inequality.

items.title: 5G mirage: Sam George blasts Akufo-Addo gov’t over zero signal two years after launch
items.description: Nearly two years after Ghana staged a high-profile launch of its fifth-generation (5G) mobile technology, consumers are still waiting to experience the service, the Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, has said. “November, this November, is exactly two years since the Akufo-Addo administration launched 5G. We are yet to see one 5G signal in this country,” he told Parliament on Tuesday, November 24, during the debate on the 2027 Budget. The Minister’s remarks have revived questions about the gap between the 2024 launch ceremony and the delivery of a service that mobile phone users can access, as the government prepares to introduce a revised framework for the rollout. President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo officially launched Ghana’s 5G initiative on November 1, 2024, at a ceremony in Accra. The project was built around Next Gen Infraco (NGIC), a wholesale infrastructure provider expected to make 5G capacity available to mobile network operators for delivery to their customers. The launch was accompanied by expectations that the technology would initially cover Accra, Kumasi and Takoradi before expanding to other parts of the country. However, Mr George said the initiative had not delivered the consumer-facing service promised to Ghanaians, nearly two years after the ceremony. He said the Mahama administration had consequently reviewed the policy governing the allocation of 5G spectrum, moving away from the previous arrangement and opening up the process to wider participation. The revised policy, he said, had enabled the government to raise $240 million through the sale of spectrum in the 700 megahertz, 2.3 gigahertz and 3 gigahertz bands. “We have sold the 5G spectrum, democratised it. We’ve raised $240 million for the Ghanaian taxpayer,” he said. Mr George said the new arrangement was intended to widen access to the technology and create opportunities for more players to participate in its deployment, while generating revenue for the state. He expressed confidence that the revised framework would accelerate the rollout, with President John Dramani Mahama expected to announce the official launch of the network before the end of this year. Consumers, he said, should begin seeing 5G signals early in 2027. “Before the end of this year, His Excellency President Mahama will announce the launch of 5G in Ghana. And by the start of next year, you will see the 5G signal,” he said. The National Communications Authority (NCA) announced in March this year that NGIC had commenced commercial operations of its shared 4G and 5G infrastructure platform, initially covering selected parts of Accra, Kumasi and Tamale. The Authority also disclosed that NGIC had installed 49 5G sites across six regions, including 43 in Greater Accra, two in Ashanti, and one each in the Western, Northern, Bono and Central regions. The wholesale network is designed to provide infrastructure that licensed mobile network operators can connect to before offering retail services to consumers. The distinction between an operational wholesale backbone and a 5G service available to subscribers is therefore central to the debate over the pace of Ghana’s rollout. In July, the NCA also removed the exclusivity clause in NGIC’s licence, opening the wholesale 5G infrastructure market to competition.

items.title: Around 175 migrants unaccounted for after contact lost with boat from Senegal
items.description: Around 175 migrants are unaccounted for after contact was lost with a Europe-bound boat that ​left the Senegalese capital Dakar about two weeks ‌ago, local officials and a human rights group said, as growing numbers attempt the perilous crossing to Europe. The boat departed from Yoff, a district of Dakar, around November 9-10, the mayor and the secretary general of the local fishing wharf said. About 175 people were travelling aboard the wooden vessel, a type known locally as a pirogue, Yoff mayor Seydina Issa Laye said. Action for Human Rights and Friendship, a non-governmental organisation, said 172 people were believed missing and called for intensified search-and-rescue efforts. Senegal’s ​navy said it had rescued 974 migrants travelling on five pirogues ‌on ⁠Monday. Navy statements show that since the beginning of November, Senegal has rescued, intercepted, or prevented more than 5,200 migrants from departing. Migrant crossings from West Africa to Europe have surged this month, according to the UN refugee agency, with more than 8,000 people arriving in the Canary Islands during the first 12 days of November. The journey is perilous and often deadly. Thousands have died attempting the crossing in recent years, including 635 ⁠in ​the first five months of this ​year, according to migrant rights group Walking Borders.

items.title: Agriculture as a strategic pillar in Ghana’s New Economy policy: Prospects, challenges and implications for educational planning
items.description: “Agriculture is the most healthful, most useful and most noble employment of man” -George Washington Historical Perspective Every nation develops a plan to guide its development. Ghana is no exception, having pursued various development plans since the colonial period to promote economic growth and social transformation. In 1919, Governor Sir Gordon Guggisberg introduced a ten-year development plan aimed at improving the Gold Coast’s economic and social infrastructure. Following independence in 1957, Ghana implemented successive development plans, including the Second Development Plan (1959–1964) and the Seven-Year Plan for National Reconstruction and Development (1963/64–1969/70). These plans prioritised economic growth, improved living standards, agriculture, industrialisation, infrastructure and social services. The Seven-Year Plan specifically promoted socialist economic transformation and incorporated the Volta River Project into Ghana’s industrialisation strategy. After the 1966 change of government, agricultural self-reliance received renewed attention through Operation Feed Yourself, launched in February 1972 to increase domestic food production and reduce food-import dependence. In 1983, Ghana launched the Economic Recovery Programme (ERP), followed by structural adjustment reforms that restored real GDP growth to approximately 5% annually during 1983–1989, supported by external financial assistance. Under the Fourth Republic (1993–present), successive development frameworks included Vision 2020, Ghana Poverty Reduction Strategies (GPRS I–II) and Ghana Shared Growth and Development Agendas (GSGDA I–II), coordinated by the National Development Planning Commission (NDPC). These frameworks prioritised poverty reduction, macroeconomic stability, agricultural modernisation, infrastructure, employment and human development, alongside social protection initiatives such as the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) and Livelihood Empowerment Against Poverty (LEAP). Despite these interventions, further efforts are needed to achieve inclusive and sustainable economic transformation. Agriculture as a Strategic Pillar in The New Economy Ghana continues to face structural economic challenges that constrain its transformation, particularly its inability to fully harness agriculture as a driver of economic growth, industrialisation and employment. Despite having fertile land, abundant water resources, favourable climatic conditions and human resources, Ghana continues to import more food than it should, rather than adequately producing what it can grow locally. The Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) reported that Ghana imported food products valued at approximately GH¢36.46 billion in 2025. This dependence highlights the gap between the country’s agricultural potential and its domestic productive capacity. Addressing this gap requires investment in irrigation, modern technology, agricultural finance, storage, processing and skilled human resources. The presentation of the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy by the Minister for Finance, Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson, on 12 November 2026 introduced a four-year economic transformation programme titled The New Economy: New Ghana, Jobs and Prosperity . Covering 2027–2030, the programme proposes an investment of US$10 billion across eight (8) strategic pillars, with commercial agriculture identified as pillar two. The Budget stated that agriculture remains important to Ghana’s economy, accounting for approximately 20% of GDP, almost 40% of employment and nearly 25% of export earnings. More so, the sector’s contribution to national development extends beyond primary production to agro-processing, transportation, trade and rural employment, Yet, the country recorded an unemployment rate of 12.8% in 2025, based on Ghana Statistical Service labour force data cited in the Budget. This contrast raises questions about the sector’s capacity to generate productive employment and its potential to contribute more substantially to national development. The US$3 billion commercial agriculture investment will target eight integrated industries: rice, sugar, poultry, maize and soya feed, aquaculture, oil palm, vegetables and cocoa value addition. These interventions are intended to expand domestic production, strengthen agro-processing, improve food security, reduce food imports and create employment. However, achieving these objectives will require more than financial investment. It will depend not only on financial investment but also on the availability of appropriately trained human resources in agricultural production, mechanisation, irrigation, research, extension services, processing, storage and marketing. This raises two central questions for educational planning: Does Ghana have the human resources and relevant technical skills required to support the proposed agricultural transformation? And do existing educational policies, curricula and institutional arrangements provide an enabling framework for developing this human capital? The capacity of universities, technical and vocational institutions, agricultural colleges and other training providers to respond to these requirements will be critical to the success of the agricultural pillar of The New Economy. Problem Context Undergraduate enrolment data for the 2026/2027 academic year from three public universities in Ghana indicate relatively low participation in agriculture-related programmes. At the University of Ghana, total undergraduate enrolment was approximately 13,949 students. The BSc Agriculture programme admitted 604 students, of whom 259 enrolled. For BSc Agricultural Engineering, 225 students were admitted, but only 26 enrolled. Combined, the two programmes accounted for approximately 2% of the university’s total undergraduate enrolment. At the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Kumasi, total undergraduate enrolment stood at 16,222 students. The BSc Agriculture programme admitted 466 students, with 260 enrolling, while BSc Agricultural Engineering admitted 144 students, of whom 78 enrolled. Together, the programmes represented approximately 2.29% of total undergraduate enrolment. At the University for Development Studies (UDS), total undergraduate enrolment was 10,517 students. The BSc Agricultural Technology programme admitted 274 students, of whom 139 enrolled, while BSc Agricultural Engineering admitted 31 students, with only 12 enrolling. Combined, these programmes accounted for approximately 1.44% of total undergraduate enrolment. These figures are based on the enrolment information available at the time of data collection and may be subject to revision as registration progresses. The figures suggest that relatively few students are enrolling in agriculture-related programmes at these selected public universities. If this pattern persists, it could constrain the supply of graduates and skilled professionals required to support the agricultural transformation envisaged under The New Economy . The difference between the number of students admitted and those who eventually enrol is also significant. This raises concerns about the factors discouraging prospective students from pursuing agriculture-related programmes, including possible negative perceptions of agriculture among young people. One possible contributing factor is the changing position of agriculture in the pre-tertiary curriculum. Agriculture was previously taught as a distinct subject at the primary, junior secondary and senior secondary levels. However, when Agriculture was incorporated into the Integrated Science curriculum, its visibility and emphasis may have diminished, potentially limiting students’ early exposure to agricultural knowledge, practical skills and career opportunities. Admission requirements for agriculture-related programmes may also influence students’ participation. Science subjects such as Physics, Chemistry, Biology and Elective Mathematics are often prioritised over agricultural subjects, including Animal Husbandry, Crop and Horticulture, Forestry and Fisheries. This may disadvantage students whose secondary-school preparation has focused on these agricultural subjects. A related concern is the reported exclusion of applicants with agricultural subject backgrounds veterinary programmes. Such admission arrangements raise questions about the recognition of agricultural education as a relevant foundation for further studies and careers in the agricultural sector. Nevertheless, practical agricultural knowledge and experience are not necessarily dependent on formal secondary or tertiary science education. Ghana has produced several award-winning farmers who have achieved considerable success without secondary education or formal science training. This demonstrates the value of practical knowledge and experience and highlights the need to recognise diverse pathways into agriculture. Admission policies, curricula and training arrangements should therefore be examined to ensure that they attract and prepare a broader range of young people for careers in the sector. Implication for Education Planning The success of The New Economy will depend largely on Ghana’s ability to develop the human resources required to implement its strategic priorities. However, a persistent challenge in the education system is the mismatch between graduates’ fields of study, their employment aspirations and the skills required by the national economy, particularly in agriculture. Many graduates continue to seek employment without the technical, practical and entrepreneurial competencies needed to respond to emerging labour-market demands. This raises important questions about the relevance of educational programmes, the alignment of curricula with national development priorities and the extent to which educational planning anticipates future skills requirements. The proposed US$3 billion investment in commercial agriculture, representing 30% of the programme’s US$10 billion investment, makes this concern particularly important. It calls for deliberate educational planning to forecast the human-resource needs of the eight targeted agricultural industries and align university, technical and vocational education, agricultural training and skills-development programmes accordingly. This does not necessarily mean allocating 30% of young people to agriculture; rather, it requires ensuring that sufficient numbers of appropriately skilled people are trained across the agricultural value chain. Educational planning is critical in this discussion as it is the systematic, data-driven process of setting goals, allocating resources, designing policies or programmes to improve how an educational system operates and serves learners. Educational planning bridges current realities such as low enrolment rates with future social, economic and learning needs. The National Development Planning Commission (NDPC), established under Articles 86 and 87 of the 1992 Constitution and operating under the National Development Planning Commission Act, 1994 (Act 479), and the National Development Planning (Systems) Act, 1994 (Act 480), has a central role in advising the President on national development planning policy and strategy. Its role is therefore critical in linking long-term national development priorities with educational planning, human-resource forecasting and institutional capacity development. The key question is how well have we empowered this strategic body to do long-term educational planning? Conclusion and Recommendations Ghana’s ambition to transform its economy through commercial agriculture requires more than financial investment; it demands a skilled human-resource base supported by effective educational planning. The agricultural pillar of The New Economy presents an opportunity to strengthen domestic production, agro-processing, food security and employment. However, its success will depend on aligning education and skills development with the sector’s human-resource needs. As Mahatma Gandhi observed, “To forget how to dig the earth and to tend the soil is to forget ourselves.” Although the programme may not resolve Ghana’s structural challenges overnight, it provides an opportunity to reposition agricultural education as the key driver of national transformation. To align educational planning with the agricultural ambitions of The New Economy , the following measures are recommended: Review academic programmes: The National Development Planning Commission (NDPC), in collaboration with the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC), should assess tertiary programmes and align them with national development priorities and projected labour-market needs, particularly in agriculture. Provide incentives for agricultural studies: Government should introduce targeted scholarships, bursaries and tuition rebates to attract more students into agriculture-related programmes. A proposed 50% tuition rebate for students in selected priority programmes could help improve enrolment. Reform programme design and admission requirements: Tertiary institutions should adopt flexible admission policies that recognise relevant agricultural subject backgrounds, introduce interdisciplinary agricultural courses and strengthen practical and entrepreneurial training. Graduates should also receive support to establish agriculture-related businesses. Strengthen pre-tertiary agricultural education: The Ministry of Education and its agencies should reconsider introducing Agriculture as a distinct compulsory subject at the pre-tertiary level to improve agricultural knowledge, practical skills and positive attitudes among young people. This will help them develop positive attitude towards subject. Support specialised agricultural institutions: Government should provide the necessary institutional and financial support to the University of Engineering and Agricultural Sciences (UEAS). The new university has the potential to transform agricultural and economic development. Dr. Paul Kwadwo Addo is an education specialist, farmer, teacher/Adjunct lecturer, Author of “Animal Husbandry for Senior High Schools” and the Registrar of the University of Engineering and Agricultural Sciences. pkaddo@yahoo.com

items.title: Two arrested after break-in at country home of Prince William and wife Kate, UK police say
items.description: Police have arrested two men on suspicion of burglary and trespass after a break-in at the country residence of Britain’s Prince William and his wife Kate, British police said on Tuesday. Norfolk Constabulary said police were called on Monday night following a report of suspicious activity at a property on the royal family’s Sandringham estate in ​Norfolk, eastern England. Dogs, drones and a helicopter were deployed to help with searches, and the force added that two men were arrested on the estate. The two men remain ⁠in custody. The Sun newspaper first reported that police were investigating a break-in at Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom ​house that the late Queen Elizabeth gave William and Kate as a wedding present in 2011. Police said ​the property was unoccupied at the time of the apparent break-in. William and Kate use the retreat for holidays and short breaks, but their main home is on the Windsor Castle estate to the west of London. A spokesperson for William ​said they did not comment on security matters. PAST ROYAL SECURITY BREACHES Several royal security incidents ​have occurred in recent years. In 2024, two masked men broke into Windsor Castle and stole two vehicles from a barn. Three years ‌earlier, a ⁠man was arrested with a loaded crossbow at Windsor Castle. He was detained for nine years after admitting making threats against the late monarch. One of the biggest breaches of royal security took place at Buckingham Palace in 1982, when an intruder climbed a wall and then wandered into the room where the queen ​was in bed. Separately on ​Tuesday, William visited Prime ⁠Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader’s office, 10 Downing Street. While the British royals often mingle with political leaders and government ministers at formal occasions, visits ​to Downing Street, the official residence of British leaders since 1735, are ​more infrequent. The late ⁠Queen Elizabeth dined with Winston Churchill at Number 10 in 1955, on the eve of his resignation, and became the first monarch for possibly 200 years to attend a cabinet meeting there in 2012 during her Diamond ⁠Jubilee year. As ​heir, King Charles also made a number of trips to ​Downing Street to attend meetings and see how the government functioned, while William’s late mother Princess Diana also visited almost exactly ​37 years ago in 1989.

items.title: Imran asks PTI to reach out to Fazl, other parties
items.description: • Core committee briefed on jailed founder’s instructions to expand political alliance • PPP urges PTI to first prove its role as effective opposition before seeking wider cooperation ISLAMABAD: The PTI’s core committee was informed that incarcerated party founder Imran Khan wanted it to expand its political alliance and reach out to JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman and other opposition parties to build a broader front. Meanwhile, the PPP played down the PTI’s invitation to join a new alliance, urging the latter to first demonstrate its role as the main opposition party inside and outside parliament. The instructions were conveyed to the core committee during an overnight meeting that began on Monday. Lawyer Latif Khosa briefed members on his meeting with Mr Khan and his wife, Bushra Bibi, at Adiala jail on Nov 11. Another of Mr Khan’s lawyers, Salman Safdar, was also present during the meeting with the couple. In a statement issued on Tuesday after the core committee meeting, the PTI said Mr Khan had expressed “complete confidence” in the opposition leadership and directed the party to expand its political alliance. New provinces Mr Khosa also briefed the core committee, chaired by PTI Chairman Barris­ter Gohar Ali Khan, on Mr Khan’s inst­r­uctions regarding the creation of new provinces. The committee was told that Mr Khan wanted the matter to be “deliberated up­­on in detail at the forthcoming meeting of PTI’s parliamentary party”. Recom­me­ndations would subsequently be prese­n­ted to him for a decision, the statement said. The committee expressed serious concern over Mr Khan’s health and demanded implementation of the Supreme Court’s Aug 18 order directing authorities to transfer him to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad. It also called for the implementation of judicial orders concerning Bushra Bibi’s medical treatment. Referring to a recent letter written by Mr Khan to top judges, the committee urged the judiciary to take immediate notice of his concerns and ensure access to personal physicians for a comprehensive medical examination and treatment. The core committee condemned the continued detention of Sohail Afridi, who has been rendered non-functional as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister following the imposition of governor’s rule, and other PTI lawmakers. It criticised the extension of detention orders under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) against elected representatives and political workers. The committee appealed to the Federal Constitutional Court and its chief justice to modify the existing stay order concerning Section 3 of the MPO and provide relief to political leaders and workers who had been granted bail by the Peshawar High Court before Nov 5 but whose release orders remained unimplemented because of the stay. It also decided to observe Nov 26 as “Martyrs’ Day” to commemorate those killed during the 2024 protests. ‘Opposition’s role’ Meanwhile, PPP General Secretary Nayyer Hussain Bukhari said the party had not decided to withdraw from the federal government, although the possibility could be considered at a meeting of its Central Executive Committee in light of prevailing circumstances. He said President Asif Ali Zardari had always prioritised political reconciliation and consensus, but the PPP was also paying a “political price” for being part of the government. Mr Bukhari said the PTI had yet to respond to PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s invitation to return to parliamentary standing committees. He said the PTI was neither visible as an effective opposition in parliament nor outside it and should present a clear political agenda instead of merely raising slogans. On the issue of new provinces, he said the PPP wanted both the PML-N and the PTI to clearly announce their positions. He questioned the silence of PML-N President Nawaz Sharif, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, saying statements by PML-N ministers also reflected confusion and inconsistency. items.title: GTEC says nationwide freeze on new PhD programmes will not last beyond a month
items.description: The Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) has assured tertiary institutions that its nationwide freeze on new PhD programmes will last no longer than a month. Deputy Director-General of GTEC, Prof. Augustine Ocloo, says the directive is a temporary regulatory intervention to address growing concerns over accreditation breaches, institutional capacity, and the quality of tertiary education. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, Prof. Ocloo dismissed fears that the suspension could disrupt an entire academic year. “So, for how long, as the GTEC DG has indicated, just after the audit, and this audit wouldn’t take more than a month to complete,” he said. He explained that the Commission would still consider applications from institutions that present compelling justifications for introducing new programmes during the suspension. He cited the University of Ghana, KNUST and the University of Cape Coast as examples of institutions whose applications could be considered on merit. Prof. Ocloo also apologised for the anxiety the directive generated, explaining that such regulatory interventions were not new. “Let me add that this hold-on or freeze approach is something that the Commission uses most of the time on a case-by-case basis. It’s just that this term is nationwide.” He revealed that GTEC had encountered institutions where only about 50% of the programmes being offered were accredited. Others, he said, were admitting excessive numbers of PhD students without the requisite academic and supervisory capacity. He explained that some institutions had also failed to maintain the standards and resources that earned them initial accreditation. The Commission intends to constitute four or five teams to examine data submitted by tertiary institutions and make recommendations. “So within a week, the data would have been analysed. Recommendations would have been given to the Commission,” he said. Prof. Ocloo, however, warned that institutions found to have inadequate capacity could face restrictions on fresh admissions for up to two years. Existing students would not ordinarily be asked to abandon their programmes. He explained that departments with too many students relative to their faculty strength could be directed to suspend admissions until they had the necessary resources in place. Prof. Ocloo maintained that the Commission’s objective was not to undermine tertiary education but to protect academic standards. “I don’t think the Commission is set out to destroy tertiary education. We are there to support and make sure that quality is sustained.” GTEC Director-General Prof. Ahmed Jinapor Abdulai announced the directive on Saturday, November 21, at the 19th Congregation of the University of Mines and Technology (UMaT) in Tarkwa. The Commission later clarified that the suspension targets applications to accredit new PhD programmes and does not constitute a blanket ban on admissions to existing accredited programmes. MyJoyOnline+1 The nationwide audit will examine accreditation status, student enrolment, supervisory capacity, research facilities, completion rates and the integrity of thesis examinations.

items.title: Whose life next?
items.description: THE killing of television anchor Rabia Ahsan in Rawalpindi this month revives a question Pakistan has yet to answer: how can we better protect women from those who threaten them? In August, digital media executive Hina Javed was found murdered . Last year, the killing of teenager Sana Yousaf in Islamabad and the shooting of a couple in Balochistan for choosing each other provoked public outrage. Though circumstances differ, the deaths show women may pay with their lives for asserting their independence or defying the expectations of others. As the world observes the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women today, Pakistan must also remember those whose suffering never makes headlines. According to the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, at least 470 women were killed in the name of so-called honour in 2025. Rights group Sahil recorded 3,172 cases of gender-based violence in the first half of 2026. These figures do not capture the abuse hidden by fear, financial dependence and pressure to protect family reputations. For many women, violence is not a lone incident but a prolonged pattern of intimidation, control and isolation, endured behind closed doors with little outside help. Each high-profile killing brings grief, condemnation and demands for justice. But outrage fades while the failures that allow violence to flourish remain. Hina Javed’s case illustrates this: nearly three months after her death, her trial has yet to begin, though police have submitted the investigation report. For women facing threats from husbands, relatives or rejected suitors, delays send a frightening message. Many hesitate to seek help, fearing that complaints will be dismissed as family disputes or that reporting abuse will provoke further retaliation. This year’s UN campaign calls for justice, protection for survivors and an end to impunity — goals that will remain elusive in Pakistan unless laws against violence are effectively enforced. Complaints must be taken seriously; repeated threats and stalking must trigger prompt police intervention; and investigations must proceed without political or family pressure. Officers must be trained to recognise escalating danger, particularly where earlier assaults, death threats or access to weapons are involved, and to connect women at risk with emergency protection rather than send them home. Women need accessible shelters, legal aid and financial support that make leaving an abusive situation a realistic option. Schools, families and community leaders must challenge the notion that women’s choices can sully someone’s ‘honour’. The test for Pakistan lies not in how loudly it mourns a murdered woman, but whether it acts to protect the next one while she is still alive. Published in Dawn, November 25th, 2026

items.title: Adjei-Mensah Korsah flags gaps in GH¢2.5bn Works and Housing budget, questions flood and coastal protection plans
items.description: Former Minister for Local Government and Regional Reorganisation, Martin Adjei-Mensah Korsah, has raised concerns about gaps in the government’s plans for flood control, coastal protection and water infrastructure, despite significant allocations in the 2027 Budget. In an assessment shared on Facebook on Wednesday, November 25, he said the Ministry of Works, Housing and Water Resources had received a headline allocation of GH¢2.5 billion, including GH¢820 million for northern water projects, GH¢75 million for other water infrastructure, GH¢250 million for Blekusu sea defence works and GH¢500 million for other coastal protection projects. While acknowledging the investments, the former Minister said the Budget did not sufficiently address maintenance, implementation timelines, household protection and measurable service outcomes. On flood management, he noted that 118 of 137 emergency desilting contracts had been completed, describing the progress as a tangible output. However, he said the status of several other construction projects remained unclear, with only 37 of 76 awarded contracts reported as ongoing. He also raised concerns about the resettlement of communities affected by the Akosombo spillage, noting that 295 homes were still scheduled for completion in 2027. He said the continuing programme highlighted the difference between announcing housing projects and ensuring that displaced families are safely rehoused. On coastal protection, Mr Adjei-Mensah Korsah acknowledged progress on ongoing works but pointed out that the published completion timetable for the Blekusu project extends to 2028. He called for clearer implementation plans and funding arrangements to ensure that affected communities receive adequate protection. The former Minister also questioned whether the reported GH¢226 million emergency reallocation and ongoing engineering works were sufficiently linked to long-term maintenance, catchment management and household protection standards. He said investments in flood forecasting equipment and models would have limited impact without evidence that warnings were reaching vulnerable communities and triggering timely action. On the proposed Pwalugu Dam and dredging along the White Volta, he said the interventions could help reduce flooding but cautioned that dredging decisions must be informed by hydraulic and sediment assessments. He stressed that dredging alone would not provide a complete solution and should be complemented by effective community warning systems. Mr Adjei-Mensah Korsah further argued that the sector’s construction spending should generate measurable local employment and skills development. He called on the government to demonstrate how housing and flood-control contracts would provide paid training, recognised skills and sustained opportunities for local businesses. He said the overall budget response to the sector’s challenges remained incomplete without stronger attention to maintenance, affordability, enforcement and the delivery of services to communities.

items.title: PhD Suspension: GTEC apologises for anxiety over freeze on new academic programmes
items.description: The Deputy Director-General of the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC), Prof. Augustine Ocloo, has apologised for the anxiety caused by the Commission’s directive freezing the introduction of new PhD programmes across tertiary institutions nationwide. He said the directive was not meant to disrupt tertiary education but to address growing concerns about academic standards, institutional capacity, and accreditation breaches. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, Prof. Ocloo assured tertiary institutions that the freeze would not extend beyond a month, and that the Commission expects to complete an audit of academic programmes within that period. GTEC’s directive to suspend new academic programmes is part of a broader regulatory intervention to assess tertiary institutions’ capacity to deliver quality education. However, the directive’s nationwide scope has raised concerns about its implications for academic expansion and programme development. Prof. Ocloo explained that although the Commission routinely imposes such restrictions on individual institutions, extending the measure nationwide had created anxiety. “Let me add that this hold-on or freeze approach is something that the Commission uses most of the time on a case-by-case basis. It’s just that this term is nationwide,” he explained before apologising for the anxiety the communication might have created. He clarified that the directive was not an absolute ban, adding that institutions with compelling justifications for introducing new programmes would still receive consideration. “There are human beings that work in the Commission, and they will critically analyse every situation.” Prof. Ocloo said the intervention became necessary after the discovery of worrying accreditation breaches and inadequate institutional capacity. In some instances, he said, only about half of the programmes institutions run were accredited. He also expressed concern about excessive admissions into doctoral programmes without the corresponding faculty strength and resources. “For instance, you come across an institution that admits about 52 PhD students into one programme. In fact, if you go all over the world, you hardly come across such matters.” The Deputy Director-General said some institutions had also failed to maintain the capacity they demonstrated when their programmes were initially accredited. GTEC intends to establish four or five teams to analyse data submitted by tertiary institutions and make recommendations to the Commission. Institutions found to have inadequate resources could be directed to suspend fresh admissions into affected programmes for a year or two until the necessary capacity is developed. However, Prof. Ocloo stressed that the Commission would not ordinarily demand the withdrawal of students already enrolled in those programmes. He maintained that the nationwide freeze was a temporary regulatory intervention, not an attempt to undermine tertiary education. “It’s not going to be one academic year freeze. It’s never going to. I don’t think the commission is set out to destroy tertiary education. We are there to support and make sure that quality is sustained.”

items.title: FDA targets WHO Listed Authority status as it marks 30th anniversary
items.description: The Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) is working towards attaining World Health Organisation (WHO) Listed Authority status as part of efforts to strengthen Ghana’s position in global health regulation. Chief Executive Officer of the FDA, Professor Kwabena Frimpong-Manso Opuni, announced the ambition at the launch of the Authority’s 30th anniversary celebrations in Accra on Tuesday, November 24, 2026. He said the Authority was taking steps to secure the recognition, which would further strengthen its standing among regulatory institutions meeting internationally recognised standards. “Our ambition is not simply to be an effective national regulator, but to be a trusted regulatory partner and a centre of excellence that contributes meaningfully to public health protection across Africa,” he said. The ambition builds on progress made by the FDA in strengthening its regulatory systems over the past three decades. The Authority attained WHO Maturity Level Three status in 2020, which was successfully re-benchmarked in January 2025. Its clinical trials and pharmacovigilance functions have also attained WHO Maturity Level Four. The FDA’s laboratory is accredited for 63 tests, while the Authority has been designated a Regional Centre of Excellence by the African Medicines Regulatory Harmonisation initiative, enabling it to support the training of regulators across the continent. FDA prepares for changing regulatory environment Professor Opuni said the next phase of the Authority’s development would require it to respond to an increasingly complex regulatory environment. He cited advances in medicines and therapies, artificial intelligence, digital health solutions and increasingly complex global supply chains as developments requiring stronger regulatory systems. “We must therefore ensure that the FDA does not simply preserve its achievements, but builds on them to become a more responsive, innovative, efficient, and globally respected regulatory institution,” he said. A new strategic plan covering 2026 to 2030 is expected to guide the transition, with priorities including digital regulation, modern infrastructure, staff development and stronger partnerships. Support for local pharmaceutical manufacturing The FDA also plans to strengthen its support for local pharmaceutical manufacturing as government pursues a target of producing 70 per cent of the country’s pharmaceutical needs locally. Professor Opuni said the Authority would provide the regulatory framework needed to support the growth of domestic pharmaceutical production. As it marks 30 years of operations, the FDA says maintaining public confidence will require cooperation among manufacturers, distributors, importers, health professionals and consumers.

items.title: Government assures Food and Drugs Authority of technical independence and support
items.description: The government has assured the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) of its commitment to protecting the institution’s technical independence, saying its regulatory decisions must remain free from external interference. Chief Director of the Ministry of Health, Desmond Boateng, gave the assurance on behalf of Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh at the launch of the FDA’s 30th anniversary celebrations. He said government would provide the Authority with the support and resources needed to strengthen its regulatory capacity. Mr Boateng said the FDA’s independence was essential to ensuring that decisions on the safety and quality of regulated products were guided by scientific evidence, public safety and the national interest. “As a government, we guarantee the FDA absolute technical independence in this endeavour. A trusted regulator is one whose decisions are guided solely by public safety and the national interest, free from external interference,” he said. The minister’s address also raised concerns about the circulation of illicit, counterfeit, substandard, falsified and unregistered products on the Ghanaian market. He warned that such products posed a serious threat to public health and could undermine the quality of healthcare. “The proliferation of illicit and fake products on our markets poses a direct lethal threat to unsuspecting citizens and undermines our clinical care outcomes,” he said. FDA urged to strengthen surveillance and enforcement Mr Boateng identified the growing use of social media and e-commerce platforms to market unapproved and expired products as a major regulatory challenge. He said the trend was creating gaps in oversight and exposing consumers, particularly young people, to potentially unsafe products. He therefore urged the FDA to intensify market surveillance, strengthen controls at ports and borders, expand laboratory testing and enforce sanctions under the Public Health Act, 2012 (Act 851). He also called for the adoption of modern tracking systems and digital platforms to monitor products across supply chains and help verify their authenticity. The government’s assurance comes as the FDA marks 30 years of regulating the safety and quality of products under its mandate.
